n:
*In the beginning*: Using the same phrase as the beginning of the Old Testament ({{Genesis 1:1|Genesis 1:1}}), the Gospel of John introduces Jesus Christ as the one through whom God created everything ({{John 1:3|John 1:3}}). Through Jesus, God also creates new life in those who believe ({{John 1:12-13|1:12–13}}). 

The Gospel of John begins with its central claim: Jesus Christ, the Word (*logos*), not only revealed God but was God. The Greek word *logos* means “word” or “message.” The *logos* is the Word of God, through whom God created everything, made himself known, and became human as Jesus Christ. Later Christian teaching describes the Word as the second person of the Trinity (the one who shares fully in God’s nature with the Father and the Holy Spirit).

In Greek thought, the *logos* was the rational principle that ordered the universe and made life understandable. It explained why the world had meaning and structure.

For Jewish people, the *logos* was the word of the Lord. It expressed God’s wisdom and God’s creative power. God spoke, and things came into being.

By the time of Jesus, people understood the *logos* as coming from God and sharing God’s character and authority (see {{Psalm 33:6|Psalm 33:6}}, {{Psalm 33:9|9}}; {{Proverbs 8:22-31|Proverbs 8:22–31}}). John affirmed this understanding by declaring that "the Word [*logos*] became flesh and made His dwelling among us" ({{John 1:14|John 1:14}}).

John began this gospel with the words, in the beginning. These same words are used earlier in the Bible. They are the first words in the story about when God created the world (Genesis 1:1).

John called Jesus the Word. That is another name for God’s word. Jesus is the Word that was with God at the beginning of the world. He was with God from the start and in fact he is God.

Jesus is also Life and Light. He shows people who God truly is. He became a human being and lived on earth.

In John’s gospel, John the Baptist was the first witness to talk about who Jesus is. John the Baptist wanted all people to believe something. He wanted them to believe that God had come to earth through Jesus. Believing that Jesus is God makes people God’s children and part of his family.

Through Jesus, God invites everyone to receive his grace and truth.

The start of this introduction might be a poem or hymn sung by early Christians ({{John 1:1-5|1:1–5}}). 

The themes of this introduction of the Gospel of John prepare readers for the story that follows:

- The arrival of the light in the world.

- The rejection of the light.

- The gift of new life given by the light to those who believed in him.
The Word (*logos*) is God ({{John 1:1-2|1:1–2}}). Everything God does, the Word also does. Throughout his Gospel, John presents the actions of Jesus as the actions of God himself.

- *In Him was life*: Life was God’s original gift to his creatures at creation ({{Genesis 1:20-28|Genesis 1:20–28}}; {{Genesis 2:7|2:7}}). Now the *logos* gives people the possibility of new life, which comes through rebirth from God ({{John 1:13|John 1:13}}). This means receiving new life from God, not a second physical birth. It describes a spiritual beginning in which God gives people new life through faith, making them his children

- As one of his first creative acts, God brought light into the world ({{Genesis 1:3|Genesis 1:3}}). In the re-creation of humankind through Jesus Christ, God offered light and life again. Light is a key theme throughout the Gospel of John.

God created *light* and removed the *darkness* ({{Genesis 1:2-5|Genesis 1:2–5}}). The darkness resists God ({{John 3:19-21|John 3:19–21}}; {{John 12:35|12:35}}; {{Matthew 6:23|Matthew 6:23}}; {{Acts 26:17-18|Acts 26:17–18}}; {{Ephesians 4:17-19|Ephesians 4:17–19}}; {{Ephesians 5:7-14|5:7–14}}; {{2 Peter 1:19|2 Peter 1:19}}; {{1 John 1:5-7|1 John 1:5–7}}; {{1 John 2:9-11|2:9–11}}).

*the darkness has not overcome it*: Or *the darkness has not understood it; *literally, *the darkness cannot grasp it*. The Greek word *katalambanō* (“grasp”) can mean either “understand” or “be hostile.” In John’s Gospel, it means "hostility." The darkness would try to destroy Jesus (the Light), but it would fail. The Light would successfully bring salvation to the world.

God sent a man named John the Baptist to announce the arrival of Jesus. He prepared people to accept Jesus as God's Son and Messiah (see {{John 1:19-37|1:19–37}}; {{Luke 1:5-25|Luke 1:5–25}}, {{Luke 1:57-80|57–80}}; {{Luke 3:1-22|3:1–22}}). His work fulfilled what God had promised through the prophets (see {{Isaiah 40:3|Isaiah 40:3}}; {{Malachi 4:5-6|Malachi 4:5–6}}).

Some Jews thought John the Baptist might be the Messiah (God's chosen one). Some of his followers hesitated to follow Jesus ({{John 3:22-30|3:22–30}}). However, John the Baptist was not the Light. His role was to announce Jesus ({{John 1:19-34|1:19–34}}).
The world does not recognize the true light, even when meeting its Creator. The world lives in rebellion, loving darkness more than light ({{John 3:19|3:19}}).

- People can follow the light and join God's family only when God spiritually renews them ({{John 3:1-17|3:1–17}}). 

- People must believe in Christ to become children of God ({{John 12:35-36|12:35–36}}).
*born of God*: People can escape the darkness only by God’s grace (see {{John 8:12|8:12}}; {{John 12:35-36|12:35–36}}, {{John 12:44-46|44–46}}).

- *The Word became flesh*: This means the Word became truly human. The idea that the Word became human was shocking to both Greeks and Jews. 

Many Greeks believed that God was completely separate from the ordinary human world. They used the word *sarx* (Greek for “flesh”) to describe human life as weak or earthly. John taught something very different. He said that God himself became human in Jesus Christ (compare {{John 1:1|1:1}}). 

Jesus was fully human and fully divine. He was not partly God and partly human. These two truths together form the foundation of Christian teaching about Christ.

- *the Word … made His dwelling among us* (Greek *skēnoō,* “pitched a tent”): The Greek verb *skēnoō* means “to pitch a tent” or “to live in a tent.” This word is related to *skēnē*, the Greek word for the tabernacle. The tabernacle was the tent where the Lord’s glory lived among Israel in the wilderness ({{Exodus 25:8-9|Exodus 25:8–9}}). In Jesus, God’s glory now lived among his people in a new way ({{Exodus 40:34-38|Exodus 40:34–38}}; {{John 2:11|John 2:11}}; {{John 12:23-28|12:23–28}}, {{John 12:41|41}}; {{John 17:1-5|17:1–5}}). 

- Even though the world was dark and hostile, Jesus came to save it. He offered God’s love and faithfulness to the world ({{John 3:15-17|3:15–17}}).

*He was before m*e: In John the Baptist’s culture, older age was respected and honored ({{Leviticus 19:32|Leviticus 19:32}}). Younger people were expected to honor those who were older, not replace them (contrast {{Isaiah 3:5|Isaiah 3:5}}). 

By saying that Jesus existed before him, John the Baptist pointed to the greater honor of Jesus. He explained that Jesus existed before creation itself, not just before the birth of John ({{John 1:1-3|John 1:1–3}}).

- *the law*: This refers to the *Torah*, the body of instruction given to Moses at Mount Sinai. The Torah taught Israel how to live in faithful relationship with God and with one another.

- God's grace and truth are present in the Torah, but Jesus fully reveals these qualities in his person and power ({{John 3:16|3:16}}; {{John 13:1|13:1}}).

- God would not allow Moses to see him directly ({{Exodus 33:18-20|Exodus 33:18–20}}). Only Jesus has seen the Father, so he alone completely knows him and can tell us about him ({{John 3:32-35|John 3:32–35}}; {{John 14:9-10|14:9–10}}). 

- *but the one and only Son*: The Son, who sees the Father, *is himself God. *The Son is not simply a messenger who knows something about God. John explicitly affirms Christ’s deity. Jesus shares the substance of God’s being.

People in Israel asked John the Baptist questions that showed they were expecting someone important.

They had been waiting for the Messiah or someone like Elijah the prophet.

But John the Baptist said he wasn’t either of those people.

A prophecy in the book of Isaiah had talked about a messenger.

John the Baptist said he was that messenger.

His message was that Jesus is God’s Chosen One.

This means that God chose Jesus to be the Saviour of the world.

John the Baptist called Jesus the Lamb of God.

At the first Passover, the Israelites were saved from death by the blood of lambs.

Jesus would save people from being slaves to sin.

This is how he was like the lambs that the Israelites sacrificed.

Jesus would take away the sins of the Israelites and of the whole world.

John the Baptist’s purpose was to be a witness about who Jesus is.

John’s Gospel focuses less on John the Baptist compared to the Synoptic Gospels ({{Matthew 3:1-6|Matthew 3:1–6}}; {{Mark 1:2-6|Mark 1:2–6}}; {{Luke 1:1-24|Luke 1:1–24}}, {{Luke 1:57-80|57–80}}; {{Luke 3:1-13|3:1–13}}). However, the apostle John wants us to understand that John the Baptist correctly identified and honored Jesus. 

John the Baptist’s disciples leave him to follow Jesus. Jesus continued the work that John had begun. As the ministry of Jesus grew, John’s ministry became smaller, just as John had said ({{John 3:30|John 3:30}}).

Jesus reveals himself to the world through his miracles and teachings. People reacted differently:

- Some wanted to believe in him.

- Others opposed him. 

This division becomes more obvious as the book continues. Jesus ended his public ministry with a final call for people to believe in him ({{John 12:44-50|12:44–50}}).

The Jews expected the Christ (the Greek form of the Hebrew word *Messiah*) to bring spiritual leadership and political redemption to Israel. Both words mean “Anointed One” (a king chosen and set apart by God). They believed this promised leader would guide them back to faithful worship and free them from foreign rule (see {{Deuteronomy 18:15|Deuteronomy 18:15}}; see also the Jewish book *Psalms of Solomon *from the period between the Old and New Testaments).

- The people expected Elijah to come before the Messiah ({{Malachi 4:5|Malachi 4:5}}). John the Baptist fulfilled this role as the forerunner (the one who prepares the way). However, John said that he was not Elijah himself (see {{Matthew 11:14|Matthew 11:14}}; {{Luke 1:17|Luke 1:17}}). 

- *Are you the Prophet?*: Compare {{John 6:14|John 6:14}}; {{John 7:40-41|7:40–41}}.
*Who are you?*: John the Baptist wanted others to know him as *a voice of one calling in the wilderness* (see {{Isaiah 40:3|Isaiah 40:3}}).

The Pharisees were deeply devoted to the Scriptures and earnestly desired a righteous life. They also believed in the coming Messiah, which explains their questions here. 

Some Pharisees became followers of Jesus, including the apostle Paul ({{Acts 15:5|Acts 15:5}}; {{Acts 26:5|26:5}}; {{Philippians 3:5|Philippians 3:5}}).

- Jewish baptisms were ritual washings for becoming ceremonially pure following contact with impurity ({{Leviticus 8:6|Leviticus 8:6}}; {{Numbers 19:7|Numbers 19:7}}). 

- John announced the Christ's arrival and required participants to confess their sins and be baptized ({{Matthew 3:6|Matthew 3:6}}). Baptism later became the symbol of membership in the kingdom of God ({{Acts 2:38|Acts 2:38}}; see also {{John 4:1-2|John 4:1–2}}).
A slave usually did simple tasks like removing a sandal. A disciple never did these tasks.

The phrase *the Lamb of God* may refer to the Passover sacrifice of a lamb or to the daily sacrifice in the temple ({{Exodus 29:38-46|Exodus 29:38–46}}; {{Hebrews 10:1-39|Hebrews 10}}). See also {{Revelation 5:1-14|Revelation 5}}.

- John the Baptist's second testimony (see {{John 1:19-23|1:19–23}}) describes what happened when he baptized Jesus . 

- In the Old Testament, kings and prophets were anointed with the Holy Spirit. These anointings were temporary. They were given for a specific task or time.

By contrast, the Spirit remained on Jesus. His anointing was not temporary. It was permanent (see {{John 3:34|3:34}}).
*the Son of God*: Some ancient manuscripts read “the Chosen One of God,” which echoes {{Isaiah 42:1|Isaiah 42:1}}, where God speaks of his chosen servant.

Two of John the Baptist’s disciples wanted to know more about Jesus.

When Jesus noticed them following him, he stopped and talked with them. This is how Jesus started to gather a group of trusted friends around him. They would learn from him, follow him and obey him.

This group began with Andrew, Simon Peter, Philip and Nathanael. These men understood that Jesus is the Messiah that God had promised to send. They told other people about him too.

At first Nathanael doubted that Jesus could be the Messiah. But after he saw and talked with Jesus, he believed Jesus was the Son of God. He called Jesus the King of Israel. Nathanael was the second witness to Jesus in John’s gospel.
This section introduces the model for discipleship in John’s Gospel. Disciples wanted to come and see Jesus, and when they met him, they stayed with him ({{John 1:39|1:39}}).

Simon is well known in the Gospels, not for his courage and faith, but for his failings (see {{John 18:15-18|18:15–18}}, {{John 18:25-27|25–27}}). Jesus gave him the name *Cephas*, an Aramaic word that means “rock.” In Greek, this name is *Petros*. In English, we say Peter. This name pointed to the strong church leader Simon would later become (see {{Acts 1:1-5:42|Acts 1:1–5:42}}; {{Acts 8:1-12:25|8:1–12:25}}; {{Acts 15:1-41|15:1–41}}).

- Galilee was the region of northern Israel around the Sea of Galilee.

- Bethsaida was a village on Galilee's north shore. The name *Bethsaida* means "house of fishing." It was the home of Peter, Andrew, and Philip. Later, Andrew and Peter moved to Capernaum, a village west of Bethsaida ({{Mark 1:21|Mark 1:21}}, {{Mark 1:29|29}}).

- Philip, a Greek name, and Nathanael, a Hebrew name, represent the mix of cultures in Galilee. The message of Jesus reached both groups in Galilee. When Greeks wanted to see Jesus in Jerusalem, they asked Philip ({{John 12:20-22|12:20–22}}). 

- Jesus grew up in Nazareth, a mountain village southwest of the Sea of Galilee.
*Can anything good come from Nazareth?*: People did not think this village was important enough to be the hometown of a great leader (see {{Matthew 13:53-58|Matthew 13:53–58}}).

Jesus described Nathanael as *a true Israelite*. He said there was no deceit (no dishonesty or trickery) in him.

This may contrast Nathanael with Jacob, whose early life was marked by deceit. Jacob later received the name *Israel* (see {{Genesis 25:27-34|Genesis 25:27–34}}; {{Genesis 27:1-36|27:1–36}}; {{Genesis 32:22-32|32:22–32}}). In this way, Nathanael shows what God desires Israel to be. God wants his people to be an honest and faithful people.

Jesus gained Nathanael’s attention by showing that he knew his character ({{John 1:47|1:47}}). Then Jesus showed that he knew Nathanael’s earlier actions, even though they had not met before.

This supernatural knowledge (knowledge beyond normal human ability) amazed Nathanael. He saw this as a sign from God and responded with faith.

Nathanael had witnessed a miracle. As a result, he made a strong confession about who Jesus is.

- *Truly, truly* (Greek *amēn amēn*): Jesus often used this phrase to emphasize important points. In John’s Gospel, the Greek word *amēn* is always doubled. 

- *you will all see heaven open*: Jesus made the comparison with Jacob clear (see study note on 1:47; see {{Genesis 28:10-22|Genesis 28:10–22}}). Like Jacob, Nathanael would see God at work. Jacob saw a vision at Bethel, where God revealed himself ({{Genesis 28:19|Genesis 28:19}}). 

Jesus himself is the new Bethel. The name *Bethel* means “house of God.” In other words, Jesus is the place where God now lives among his people.

- *Son of Man*: See study note on John 9:35; see also {{Daniel 7:13-14|Daniel 7:13–14}}; {{Mark 8:31|Mark 8:31}}. 

- John the apostle used several names for Jesus (Son of God, Son of Man, Christ). Knowing the true identity of Jesus is necessary to fully understanding and following him.
*Wedding* ceremonies could last up to a week. They often included dramatic parades where the husband brought the bride to his home for the celebrations ({{Matthew 25:1-13|Matthew 25:1–13}}).

In his gospel, John wrote about seven signs that Jesus performed. These were miracles that showed that he is the Messiah.

The first sign was when Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding. Wine was very important at Jewish weddings during that time. Not having enough wine was a cause of shame.

At first, Jesus didn’t want to do anything about the wine. It wasn’t time to show everyone who he was. He called his mother dear woman when he explained this.

But Mary trusted him to do something about the wine anyway. And Jesus did. He turned a very large amount of water into good wine.

When the disciples saw this sign, they believed that Jesus came from God.

In this section, Jesus appeared at two symbolic Jewish ceremonies. At a wedding in Cana ({{John 2:1-12|2:1–12}}), he replaced the ritual cleansing water with his own superior wine. Later, around Passover, he cleansed the temple ({{John 2:13-25|2:13–25}}).

Jesus showed who he is and what he came to do through the religious practices and festivals of the Jewish people (see {{John 2:1|2:1}}; {{John 5:1|5:1}}). He used these familiar events to reveal his identity and his mission.

- When the wine supply ran out, the host’s family would face embarrassment for failure to plan properly. Perhaps Jesus arrived unexpectedly with his disciples (see {{Matthew 25:1-13|Matthew 25:1–13}}). This might explain why his mother told him about the problem. 

- A wedding feast was a major celebration in Jewish village life. This particular event also symbolized the joy of the Messiah's arrival.

- At first, Jesus did not step in to solve the problem. His mission and its timing were not controlled by human plans.

- *My hour has not yet come*: This refers to the time when Jesus would be glorified. In the Gospel of John, this happened when he was lifted up on the cross ({{John 12:23|12:23}}; {{John 17:1|17:1}}).

The stone water jars were cut from solid rock. They were used for Jewish purification ceremonies (religious washing rituals; see {{Mark 7:1-4|Mark 7:1–4}}).

Jesus was about to give new meaning to these ceremonies. He would show that something greater than ritual washing was now present.

The master of the banquet repeated a common saying. Normally, the best wine was served first, when people could taste it most clearly. Later, wine of lower quality was served.

But this time it was different. The wine Jesus made, served last, was the best of all.

In the Old Testament, good wine was a sign of God’s blessing({{Amos 9:13-14|Amos 9:13–14}}). This miracle showed that the Messiah, God’s greatest blessing, had now come.
*Jesus performed this, the first of His signs*: In it, he revealed the glory of God (see also {{John 1:14|1:14}}; {{John 11:4|11:4}}, {{John 11:40|40}}).

The Jewish Passover was an annual spring feast remembering Israel’s rescue from slavery in Egypt ({{Exodus 12:1-51|Exodus 12}}). Jews traveled to Jerusalem to join the feast ({{Deuteronomy 16:1-16|Deuteronomy 16:1–16}}). Because John refers to three Passover feasts ({{John 2:13|John 2:13}}; {{John 6:4|6:4}}; {{John 11:55|11:55}}), many scholars think Jesus must have had a three-year public ministry.

In Jesus’ time, the temple in Jerusalem was the most important building in Israel.

People went to the temple to pray and to worship God. They would admit their sins and make sin offerings. But Jesus saw that people had turned the temple into a marketplace. This made him very angry.

Jesus showed that he had authority over what happened in the temple. The Jewish leaders challenged him about this. Jesus answered by talking about a new temple that he would build in three days. No one understood what he meant. They didn’t understand that Jesus was talking about himself.

He would be the sacrifice for people’s sin when he died on the cross. Then after three days he would be raised from the dead. His body would be the new temple. Now people pray and worship God through Jesus.

- Many people came to Jerusalem for the Passover festival. They needed animals that met the requirements for sacrifice. The animals had to be approved for worship.

Because of this need, a large business developed. People sold animals and exchanged money for the right kind of coins. However, this buying and selling was taking place in the temple itself.

Jesus acted like a prophet. He demanded that God’s house return to its true purpose. The temple was meant for worship, prayer, teaching, and sacrifice. It was not meant to be a marketplace. This action brought Jesus into conflict with the temple leaders.

- The Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, and Luke) place the clearing out of the temple near the end of the ministry of Jesus ({{Matthew 21:12-13|Matthew 21:12–13}}; {{Mark 11:15-17|Mark 11:15–17}}; {{Luke 19:45-46|Luke 19:45–46}}). John might have included this event earlier to emphasize its connection to the miracle where Jesus turned water into wine ({{John 2:1-11|John 2:1–11}}). Both the temple and the stone jars of water were instruments for spiritual purity in Judaism. The jars, once filled with water for ceremonial washing, now held the wine Jesus changed by a miracle. 

In a similar way, the stone temple, which was linked to sacrifice and purification, would no longer be central. Jesus himself would take its place ({{John 2:19-21|2:19–21}}). 

Some scholars believe that Jesus cleansed the temple twice. They think he did this once at the beginning of his ministry and again at the end.

*Destroy this temple*: Herod the Great started rebuilding the temple's grand structure in 20 BC. The work continued until AD 64. This is why Jesus amazed his audience when he claimed he could destroy and rebuild it in a few days. 

However, Jesus was speaking figuratively (using a word picture) about his own body. He described his body as the true temple, the place where God was present (see {{John 1:14|1:14}}, {{John 1:51|51}}). 

His body would be destroyed. Three days later, God would raise him from the dead. Through his resurrection, Jesus showed that he himself was now the true place where people meet God. Because of this, the Jerusalem Temple and its sacrifices were no longer necessary.

Later, during the trial of Jesus, some people misunderstood his words. They used his statement about destroying the temple as evidence against him. They accused him of blasphemy ({{Mark 14:58|Mark 14:58}}).

*they believed*: Seeing a miracle from God can lead people to believe. However, this kind of belief is not the deepest faith. The deepest faith trusts Jesus even without seeing miracles ({{John 20:29|20:29}}).

John uses a play on words here. Because of Jesus’s signs (miracles that show who he is), many people trusted in him ({{John 2:23|2:23}}). But Jesus did not trust them in the same way.

This statement does not refer only to certain people in Jerusalem. It shows that Jesus knows what is inside every person. He understands people’s thoughts, motives (reasons for acting), and desires.

- John connects {{John 2:25|2:25}}{{John 3:1|John 3:1}}and{{John 3:1|3:1}} by using the same Greek word (*anthrōpos*) to refer to all of humanity and then to a specific man (Nicodemus). 

- Nicodemus had deep religious knowledge. He had also seen what Jesus was doing in Jerusalem ({{John 2:13-24|2:13–24}}). But he had not yet experienced spiritual rebirth (a new life that comes from God).

- *A Pharisee*: See study note on 1:24. The Pharisees were a Jewish group who were careful to obey the law of Moses and their religious traditions.

Nicodemus belonged to this group. He was part of the religious leaders. He was respected for his knowledge of the Jewish law. He likely took pride in his careful obedience and moral purity.

Nicodemus was searching for the truth about who Jesus was. But he didn’t understand spiritual things.

Jesus told Nicodemus that he had to be born again to enter the kingdom of God. People are born again when they believe that Jesus is God’s Son and follow him.

The Holy Spirit makes people able to receive new life from God. Jesus is God’s Light. He saves those who believe in him from the power of sin and evil.

Yet people who love evil don’t want to be near God’s Light. They want to stay in darkness instead. One day God will judge all sin and everything that is unjust. But first Jesus offers truth, life and light for the Gentiles.

*at night*: Nicodemus might have been afraid for others to see him with Jesus. In the Gospel of John, *night* often has a deeper meaning. It can represent evil, error (wrong belief), and unbelief (lack of trust in God; see {{John 9:4|9:4}}; {{John 11:10|11:10}}; {{John 13:30|13:30}}).

- *Born again: *To experience spiritual birth, God's power must completely renew a person. 

- Nicodemus thought Jesus was speaking about physical birth. He demonstrated that those in darkness, who do not have spiritual rebirth, cannot understand Jesus or other “heavenly things” ({{John 3:12|3:12}}). 

Jesus sometimes used ironic misunderstanding as a way to teach. He would say something with a deeper spiritual meaning. The listener would misunderstand his words in a simple or physical way. Then Jesus would explain the deeper meaning.

This method helped people see the difference between earthly thinking and spiritual truth.
John the Baptist baptized with water. Jesus baptizes with the Holy Spirit ({{John 1:33|1:33}}).
In Greek, the word for *wind* is the same as for *spirit* (Greek *pneuma*). The wind is an appropriate image for the Spirit, who is sent from heaven and cannot be contained or controlled.

There is a great distance between this world and heaven (see {{John 1:51|1:51}}; {{John 3:31|3:31}}; {{John 6:38|6:38}}, {{John 6:42|42}}). Heaven represents God’s dwelling place. This world represents human life under sin and weakness.

Jesus came down from heaven to this world. He made a way for people to know God. He proved that he came from God when he defeated death. After rising from the dead, he returned to the Father in heaven ({{John 16:5-11|16:5–11}}).
Jesus was lifted up on the cross so that all people could understand the way of salvation, look to him in faith, and have eternal life.

- The truth that God loved the world is basic to Christian understanding ({{1 John 4:9-10|1 John 4:9–10}}). God's love extends beyond the limits of race and nation, even to those who oppose him (see “The World” Theme Note). 

- The Son came to save, not to condemn, people who often choose spiritual darkness ({{John 3:17|3:17, 1}}{{John 3:19-21|9–21}}).

The original Greek text does not include quotation marks. Because of this, translators must decide where the words of Jesus end and where John's explanation begins. {{John 3:16-21|John 3:16–21}} might be John’s explanation of what Jesus said.

As light shines into a dark place, it reveals what was hidden. In the same way, when Jesus came into the world, he exposed its sin and unbelief. Because of this, God’s judgment has already begun.

People who see this light and understand their true condition must respond. They are responsible to believe in God’s Son ({{John 3:16-17|3:16–17}}).

When people live in spiritual darkness (a life separated from God), they do not want the light that Jesus brings. Jesus called himself "the light of the world" ({{John 8:12|8:12}}; {{John 9:5|9:5}}). His light shows truth and exposes sin.

Darkness does not simply ignore the light. It resists it and tries to overcome it. But the darkness cannot defeat the light ({{John 1:5|1:5}}). 

Those who refuse to believe continue to live in darkness ({{John 13:30|13:30}}). They stumble because they cannot see clearly ({{John 11:10|11:10}}). In the end, their sins will be revealed. God will judge all people ({{John 5:28-30|5:28–30}}; {{Revelation 20:11-15|Revelation 20:11–15}}).
*He spent some time with them and baptized*: See {{John 4:2|John 4:2}}, which explains that the disciples of Jesus were the ones who baptized people.

John the Baptist always pointed people towards Jesus the Messiah. He was glad when more and more people began to follow Jesus and not him.

His joy didn’t come from being important. His joy came from seeing the great work of Jesus.

John the Baptist knew that Jesus is a witness to who God is. And he knew that his job was to be a witness to Jesus.

Jesus shows what God is like. The Holy Spirit is with him. Those who refuse to accept this face God’s anger. But God gives life that will last for ever to everyone who believes in Jesus.
John the Baptist says Jesus is truly "from above" ({{John 3:31|3:31}}). So, the followers of John need to start following Jesus instead.

Before King Herod imprisoned John (see {{Matthew 14:1-12|Matthew 14:1–12}}; {{Mark 1:14|Mark 1:14}}; {{Mark 6:14-29|6:14–29}}; {{Luke 3:19-20|Luke 3:19–20}}), he and Jesus were both ministering near the Jordan River. They were working in the same general area.

After John was arrested, Jesus left that region. He traveled north to Galilee and began his ministry there ({{Mark 1:14|Mark 1:14}}).
*everyone is going to Him*: Many people were going to Jesus. His growing popularity made some of John’s followers jealous.

John the Baptist spoke because of two concerns: 

- Some people questioned whether his baptism was from God (see {{John 1:26|1:26}}), and

- his disciples were worried because many people were beginning to follow Jesus instead of John ({{John 3:26|3:26}}).

John the Baptist described Jesus as the bridegroom. He described himself as the bridegroom’s friend.

John did not try to bring honor to himself. Instead, he gave honor to Jesus and showed that Jesus is greater than he is.
Jesus came from heaven. Because of this, he alone was able to make the Father known ({{John 1:18|1:18}}; {{John 3:13|3:13}}).

*God gives the Spirit without limit*: The Father shows his deep love for the Son ({{John 3:35|3:35}}). This also shows the divine nature of Jesus. John presents the one God as three persons (compare {{1 John 5:5-12|1 John 5:5–12}}).

- God gives the gift of eternal life. This life is not only about the future. It begins now. It is a new life and a close relationship with God in the present.

- *Whoever rejects the Son will not see life*: The world, living in darkness and sin, already stands under God’s judgment ({{Romans 1:1-3:31|Romans 1–3}}). This judgment shows God’s anger against sin and evil.

Jesus went from Judea in the south of Israel to Galilee in the north. In between them was the area of Samaria. The people who lived there in Jesus’ time were called Samaritans.

Jews thought that they were more a part of Abraham’s family than the Samaritans. Most Samaritans and Jews hated one another and tried hard to avoid each other. Jesus didn’t hate Samaritans or avoid them. He asked a Samaritan woman for water. She didn’t understand right away what he was talking about. She was thinking about things she could see and touch. But Jesus was speaking about spiritual things.

He talked about water, mountains and other things as signs of spiritual truths. People’s spirits need life from Jesus just like their bodies need water. Jesus brings eternal life to people. He described this like bringing water to people who are thirsty. He taught that all people could worship God. They could do this with the Spirit’s help. There wasn’t only one place to worship. Those who believe that Jesus is the Messiah are true worshippers of God. This was true for Jews and Samaritans and it’s true for everyone.

Jesus knew everything about the life of the woman he talked with. Most Jews wouldn’t have accepted her because she was a Samaritan. Her relationships with men were not the way the Law of Moses taught that they should be. Yet Jesus invited her to receive living water from him.

- At an ancient well in Samaria, Jesus offered himself as *living water*. This *living water* means the life that comes from God. Jesus spoke openly about who he was. When he revealed God’s truth, people had to respond. They either followed him or turned away.

- The Samaritan woman is very different from Nicodemus. She was a woman, not a man. She was a Samaritan, not a Jew. She had a sinful past, not a reputation for righteousness. She was an outsider, not a respected teacher of Israel.

Nicodemus came to Jesus at night and did not openly respond to the challenges from Jesus ({{John 3:1-21|3:1–21}}). The Samaritan woman spoke with Jesus in the daylight. She recognized him as Lord. She remained in the light and showed signs of becoming a disciple (see {{John 1:35-51|1:35–51}}).

Jesus himself did not baptize anyone with water. He allowed his disciples to perform water baptism.

Later, after he was lifted up on the cross and then raised from the dead, Jesus returned to the Father. This suffering, death, resurrection, and return to the Father is called his glorification ({{John 7:37-39|7:37–39}}). After this, Jesus baptized people in the Holy Spirit ({{John 1:33|1:33}}; {{Acts 2:4|Acts 2:4}}).
After John the Baptist had been imprisoned, Jesus left Judea (see {{Mark 6:14-29|Mark 6:14–29}}; compare {{Mark 1:14|Mark 1:14}}).

- When traveling north to Galilee, Jesus chose the less common route through Samaria. Samaria and Judea had a long history of racial tension (see {{2 Kings 17:24-41|2 Kings 17:24–41}}; {{Ezra 4:1-5|Ezra 4:1–5}}; {{Nehemiah 4:1-23|Nehemiah 4}}; {{Nehemiah 6:1-19|6:1–19}}). In the time of Jesus, there was intense racial and cultural conflict between Jews and Samaritans. Jews usually avoided Samaria by first going east to Jericho and then traveling north through the Jordan Valley. 

- Sychar was likely in the area of Shechem. Jesus arrived at Jacob's well. Jacob had owned land near Shechem ({{Genesis 33:18-19|Genesis 33:18–19}}).

Due to the heat, it was customary for the women to draw water in early morning or evening. However, this woman lived in isolation, separated from her community. Jesus was compassionate toward outcasts.

The woman was surprised. Social taboos (strict cultural rules about proper behavior) would normally prevent a Jewish teacher like Jesus from speaking to her ({{John 4:18|4:18}}). But Jesus did not allow these social rules to control him. He chose to speak with her and offer what she truly needed.

Shechem had no rivers. So it had no *living water,* which usually means fresh, flowing water from a stream or spring (see “Living Water” Theme Note). However, Jesus was speaking symbolically. The gift he offered was not ordinary water. It was the Holy Spirit, whom God would give to believers ({{John 7:37-39|7:37–39}}).

Jacob’s well was more than 30 meters (about 100 feet) deep. A person needed a long rope and a container to draw water from it.

The woman focused on the physical water in the well. She did not yet understand the deeper meaning of what Jesus was saying. At that time, she was still in spiritual darkness.
*Our father Jacob*: The Samaritan woman respected the holy traditions related to the well more than the presence of God in front of her.

In the dry climate of Israel, a fresh, bubbling spring was a strong and hopeful image. Flowing water meant life, safety, and relief from thirst.

The prophets used this image to describe God’s care. They said that those who come to God will not hunger or thirst (see {{Isaiah 49:10|Isaiah 49:10}}; {{Isaiah 55:1-3|55:1–3}}; {{Jeremiah 2:13|Jeremiah 2:13}}).
The woman asked Jesus for this water, but she did not understand the spiritual meaning of his words. To overcome this spiritual barrier, Jesus spoke about her sin ({{John 4:16-18|4:16–18}}).

The woman’s immoral life affected her understanding. Her pattern of broken relationships kept her from seeing clearly.

She had been married five times. She was also living with a man who was not her husband. These facts show that her life did not match God’s will. Her sin created a barrier between her and a full understanding of what Jesus was saying.

- *a prophet*: Jesus revealed knowledge about the woman that a stranger could not know ({{John 4:16-18|4:16–18}}; compare {{John 1:48|1:48}}). 

- As the woman learned more about Jesus, what she called him showed her increasing understanding:

- At first, she recognized him as "a Jew" ({{John 4:9|4:9}}) and called him "Sir" ({{John 4:11|4:11}}, {{John 4:15|15}}, {{John 4:19|19}}). 

- Later, she thought he might be "the Christ" ({{John 4:29|4:29}}), that is, the Messiah (God's chosen one). 

- Finally, the people of the village recognized him as "the Savior of the world" ({{John 4:42|4:42}}). 

Her growing understanding of the identity of Jesus is a lesson for John’s audience (see {{John 20:31|20:31}}).

The woman did not answer the moral questions that Jesus asked her. Instead, she changed the subject.

She began to speak about the long-standing division between Jews and Samaritans. This conflict included differences about worship and history. By raising this issue, she moved the conversation away from her personal life.

The Samaritans worshiped on Mount Gerizim. This mountain rises above the city of Shechem.

Both Mount Gerizim and Shechem were important places in the Old Testament (see {{Genesis 12:6-7|Genesis 12:6–7}}; {{Genesis 33:19|33:19}}; {{Deuteronomy 11:29|Deuteronomy 11:29}}; {{Joshua 8:33|Joshua 8:33}}; {{Joshua 24:1|24:1}}, {{Joshua 24:25|25}}, {{Joshua 24:32|32}}).

- Jesus affirmed that the Jews had preserved the correct understanding of the one true God whom they worshiped.

- God chose the Jewish people for a special relationship with himself. He gave them his law, his promises, and his covenant (promises between God and his people). The Messiah (God’s chosen one) was to come from the Jewish people (see also {{Romans 9:4-5|Romans 9:4–5}}).

*in spirit and in truth*: In Greek, one preposition (a connecting word) is used for both words. This shows that *spirit and truth* form one united idea.

True worship happens when God’s Spirit makes God’s truth known to a person. Worship is not only about a place or a ceremony. It is about responding to God with the help of his Spirit and according to what is true about him.

Jesus himself is the Truth ({{John 14:6|14:6}}). The Spirit is also called the Spirit of truth ({{John 14:17|14:17}}; {{John 15:26|15:26}}). Together, the Spirit and the Truth make true worship possible.

*I who speak to you am He*: Jesus used an unusual and strong form of the words *I am*.

This wording may point beyond a simple statement of identity. It can suggest a connection with the name of God revealed in the Old Testament (see {{John 8:58|8:58}}; {{Exodus 3:14|Exodus 3:14}}).

The woman was not fully certain about who Jesus was ({{John 4:29|4:29}}). She asked the people of her village, *“Could this be the Christ?”* Her words show that she was still thinking and learning.

Even so, she ran back to the village and told others about him. She invited them to come and see for themselves.

Telling others about Jesus is a sign of discipleship. Earlier in this Gospel, others also invited people to “come and see”(see {{John 1:39|1:39}}, {{John 1:46|46}}).

Jesus talked about food and harvests to teach his disciples about spiritual truths. He told them what his most important food was. It was the work his Father gave him to do. Obeying his Father gave Jesus spiritual strength the way that food gave his body strength.

Other workers like John the Baptist had helped prepare people for when Jesus came. These workers were the ones who planted. Those who believed in Jesus were the plants being harvested. Jesus’ disciples were busy gathering the plants that others had worked hard to plant. The Samaritans were being harvested.

The people in the town believed what the woman told them about Jesus. Even though Jesus was a Jew, the Samaritans wanted him to stay in their village. That wasn’t the way that Jews and Samaritans usually treated one another. When the Samaritans believed Jesus’ words they were changed. They understood that Jesus is the Saviour not only of the Jews. He is the Saviour of everyone who hears his message and believes in him.

While Jesus spoke to the Samaritan woman, the disciples had gone to buy food ({{John 4:8|4:8}}). When they returned, they urged Jesus to eat. Jesus spoke with symbolic language, but they did not understand him ({{John 4:33|4:33}}). 

Later, when the disciples received the Holy Spirit, they understood what he meant ({{John 2:22|2:22}}). Jesus sustained himself spiritually by doing what his Father told him to do (see {{John 5:30|5:30}}; {{John 6:38|6:38}}; {{John 7:18|7:18}}; {{John 8:50|8:50}}; {{John 9:4|9:4}}; {{John 10:37-38|10:37–38}}; {{John 12:49-50|12:49–50}}).

*four months until the harvest*: Jesus referred to a common saying about farming. Farmers usually waited about four months between planting seed and gathering the crop.

In Samaria, it was likely the time of harvest, and the fields were ready to be gathered. Jesus used this picture to speak about people, not crops.

He had spoken with the woman at the well and planted spiritual seed (God’s message). Soon after, many Samaritans believed in him ({{John 4:39-42|4:39–42}}). In this way, Jesus was already gathering a harvest of faith.
*others*: Jesus might have meant John the Baptist. Or, he might have been referring to the work he had just done with the Samaritan woman.

*Many of the Samaritans*: The religious leaders and teachers in Jerusalem did not respond to Jesus with faith (chapter {{John 3:1-36|3}}). In contrast, many Samaritans believed in him. They first listened because of the testimony (public witness) of this woman, who had been an outsider in her community. Later, they believed because they heard Jesus for themselves.

The Samaritans had heard Jesus and believed his message for themselves. They were no longer depending only on the woman’s testimony.

They called him *Savior of the world* (see also {{1 John 4:14|1 John 4:14}}). This title shows that they understood something important. Salvation was not limited to one ethnic group.

As Samaritans, they knew they were separated from the Jews. Yet they recognized that Jesus came for all people. His mission was not only for Jews, but for the whole world ({{John 1:4-12|John 1:4–12}}; compare {{John 12:20-26|12:20–26}}).

After two days in Samaria, Jesus returned to the area of Galilee. He went back to Cana where he had changed the water into wine.

Jesus also did his second sign in Cana. An official of Herod Antipas heard that Jesus was there. The official’s son was dying. He believed that Jesus had the power to heal his son.

Jesus challenged him to have even greater faith. He told the official that his son would live. The man went away trusting that Jesus spoke the truth.

Later the official learnt that his son had been healed. It had happened at the exact time when Jesus spoke to the official. After that, the official and his whole family trusted in Jesus and followed him. This sign showed Jesus’ power over illness and death.

Unlike many people in Jerusalem, the Galileans welcomed Jesus when he came to them.

However, their welcome was based on amazement at his miracles (see {{John 2:23-25|2:23–25}}). They were impressed by what he did.

This response was not yet true faith. True faith trusts in who Jesus is, not only in the signs and wonders he performs.
Jesus strongly criticized the Galileans for asking to see miracles and wonders before they would believe (see {{John 6:30|6:30}}).
*"Your son will live"*: Jesus also healed the centurion’s servant and the Phoenician woman’s daughter from a distance ({{Matthew 8:5-13|Matthew 8:5–13}}; {{Matthew 15:21-28|15:21–28}}).
Like many other people, the Jewish official and his household believed in Jesus because of the miracle ({{John 2:23|2:23}}; {{John 4:39|4:39}}).

*the second sign … in Galilee*: Two miracles at Cana frame for this section of John's Gospel ({{John 2:11|2:11}}; {{John 4:46|4:46}}). The first miracle was when Jesus turned water into wine. The second was when he healed the official’s son. These two events mark the beginning and the end of this part of the story.

*a feast of the Jews*: Jesus returned to Jerusalem for this celebration. Because of this, it was likely one of the three main pilgrimage festivals (special festivals when people traveled to Jerusalem).

In the Old Testament, God commanded Israel to celebrate three such festivals each year (see {{Exodus 23:14-17|Exodus 23:14–17}}; {{Deuteronomy 16:16|Deuteronomy 16:16}}). These were the Feast of Unleavened Bread (also called Passover), the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Tabernacles.

Each of these festivals lasted about one week. During that time, many people gathered in Jerusalem to worship God.

The pool of Bethesda was a famous place of healing. Many people stayed close to the pool hoping to be healed from their suffering.

On a Sabbath day Jesus healed one of the men lying by the pool. This was the third sign Jesus did. It led to conflict between Jesus and the Jewish leaders.

The man Jesus healed was carrying the mat he had been lying on. This went against one of the Jewish laws about the Sabbath day. That law wasn’t part of the Ten Commandments or the Law of Moses.

Jesus didn’t agree with the extra rules that the Jewish leaders tried to make the people obey. His work was to free people from the power of sin. His work was also to bring healing to their bodies. Setting people free was more important than whether people carried things around on the Sabbath day.

The Jewish leaders wanted to know who had healed the man. After the man met Jesus in the temple, he told the leaders it was Jesus.

This chapter is structured like a courtroom case (a legal trial). It begins with a description of the event that led to the conflict ({{John 5:1-15|5:1–15}}). This is followed by the decision of the Jewish leaders to take action against Jesus ({{John 5:16|5:16}}). Next comes a statement of the charges against him ({{John 5:18|5:18}}). The chapter then presents the defense given by Jesus, where he explains his authority and his relationship with the Father ({{John 5:17|5:17}}, {{John 5:19-40|19–40}}).

In this section, Jesus attends several Jewish feasts and uses their imagery to reveal deeper truths about himself. 

He appears at:

- a Sabbath feast (chapter {{John 5:1-47|5}}),

- Passover (chapter {{John 6:1-71|6}}),

- the Feast of Tabernacles (chapters {{John 7:1-9:41|7–9}}), and

- the Feast of Dedication (also called Hanukkah; chapter {{John 10:1-42|10}}). 

In each case, Jesus himself replaces an important element in the ceremonies of the feast.

Greek copyists who had never been to Jerusalem had difficulty interpreting and spelling the name Bethesda, so there are several variants of this name in the manuscripts. The best choice is *Beth-esda*, which means “house of flowing.”

- The pool of Bethesda was a place for healing where many sick people gathered. They hoped God would cure them with a miracle. 

- Some later manuscripts include an additional verse, John 5:4, which explains that an angel stirred the water. This verse is not included in the Berean Standard Bible because it does not appear in the earliest manuscripts of the Gospel of John. The added verse reflects an early tradition that helps explain why people gathered at the pool.

No organized care system existed to help this man. He had been sick for 38 years.

He likely could not keep himself clean. He probably could not move easily on his own. Most likely, he depended on begging from people who came to the pool (see {{John 5:7|5:7}}). From a human point of view, his situation seemed hopeless.

- Jesus healed the sick man immediately and only asked him to obey. To prove that the man was healed, Jesus told him to pick up his mat and walk.

- Jesus performed this miracle on the Sabbath. The Sabbath was a weekly day of rest. The law of Moses said that no work should be done on that day (based on {{Genesis 2:2|Genesis 2:2}}; {{Exodus 20:8|Exodus 20:8}}). Jewish tradition identified 39 types of work that were not allowed (*Mishnah Shabbat* {{John 7:2|7:2}}). One rule said that a person could not carry an object, such as a sleeping mat, from one place to another ({{John 5:10|John 5:10}}). 

Jesus told the healed man to pick up his mat and walk. When the man obeyed Jesus, he broke this later Jewish tradition.

*Who is this man who told you*: The focus of the story now changes. It moves from the joy of a miracle to an accusation about breaking the Sabbath.

The religious leaders wanted to know who told the man to carry his mat. They asked for the name of the healer who had broken their tradition.
*Stop sinning*: Although Jesus healed this man physically, the man still needed to learn to obey the Lord. The man's next action ({{John 5:15|5:15}}) might indicate that he did not listen.

The Jewish leaders thought that Jesus dishonoured their rules by healing people on the Sabbath day. They also thought that he dishonoured God by calling God his Father. They wanted to kill him for doing these things.

Jesus explained to the religious leaders that he did his work to please God. He wanted them to understand his relationship with his Father. Jesus and his Father love each other and depend on one another. Jesus was doing on earth the work he saw his Father doing. This work was to save God’s world.

Some people refuse to believe that Jesus comes from God. They refuse to receive the life that God wants to give them. Jesus will give life that can’t be destroyed to everyone who believes in him. They will be saved from death and judgement. They will enjoy life for ever with God.

The religious leaders thought that they honoured God by obeying all the rules they made. But to really honour God they needed to honour Jesus.

*My Father is at His work, and I too am working*: The Sabbath was a day of rest. People were not supposed to work.

However, Jewish teachers agreed that God still worked on the Sabbath. God gives life through birth. God also takes life in death. God’s work does not stop.

Jesus used this idea to explain his actions. He said that, like his Father, he was also working. By speaking this way, Jesus compared himself with God.

The Jewish leaders understood what he meant. They objected because they believed he was claiming a special right that belongs only to God.

Jesus claimed that his work on the Sabbath was the same as God’s work on the Sabbath. Jesus claimed to be equal with God, doing the things God does. Yet he submitted to God’s will, doing only what the Father wanted.
Most Jews firmly believed in resurrection but viewed it as something God alone could accomplish. Jesus claimed that he gives life.
In addition to giving life, Jesus claimed the absolute authority to judge, which belongs to God alone.

*the Father who sent Him*: In the ancient world, a person could send an authorized representative to seal a contract or make an authoritative decision. Jesus claimed to be God’s representative, so obeying Jesus is the same as obeying God, and dishonoring him is dishonoring God.
Jesus is the giver of life as well as the judge (see {{John 5:21-22|5:21–22}}), but he never works independently of the Father.

God's law requires more than one witness in a trial ({{Deuteronomy 17:6|Deuteronomy 17:6}}). A single person’s word is not enough to prove a case.

Jesus recognized this principle. He said that his own testimony needed support from others.

So he presented several witnesses who confirmed who he was. These witnesses supported his claims and showed that his message was true.

Jesus spoke to the Jewish leaders about witnesses, truth and how to study the Scriptures. The Scriptures were another name for God’s word. The Jewish leaders had heard what John the Baptist taught. John the Baptist was like a light that pointed people to Jesus. For a while the leaders had enjoyed John’s light.

The leaders had been studying the Scriptures for a long time. They paid a lot of attention to the Law of Moses. But they had failed to understand something very important. John the Baptist, Moses and the Scriptures were all witnesses that pointed to Jesus.

Studying and learning all the Scriptures is good. But it’s Jesus who gives meaning to everything the Scriptures teach. God himself was a witness that Jesus was telling the truth about who he is.

The first witness who spoke in support of Jesus was God himself.

Jesus may have been thinking about the voice from heaven at his baptism, when God said that Jesus was his Son ({{Mark 1:11|Mark 1:11}}). He may also have meant the power of God that worked through him in his miracles.

In both ways, God gave testimony about who Jesus is.
The second witness of Jesus was John the Baptist. John pointed to Jesus and said that he is the Messiah ({{John 1:29-34|1:29–34}}).
The third witness of Jesus was his teachings and miracles. These were signs that revealed his true identity and indicated that the Father sent him.
The fourth witness of Jesus was the Scriptures. The Old Testament pointed to the Messiah, and Jesus fulfilled its prophecies (see {{Luke 24:25-27|Luke 24:25–27}}).

Jewish trials were meant to discover the truth. The goal was to decide whether the charges were true or false.

If people were falsely accused, they could show that they were innocent. He could also bring charges against those who had accused him. In this situation, Jesus did that.

Jesus said that the Jewish leaders did not have God’s love in them. They did not truly love God.

Because they did not love God, they could not understand what Jesus was doing. Without love for God, they were unable to recognize God’s work in him.

The Jewish leaders wanted honor and praise from one another. They cared about their reputation and status.

They loved religious activity, but they did not truly love God. Their actions did not match their claims. Because of this, God would judge them ({{John 5:45-46|5:45–46}}).

The fifth and final witness for Jesus was Moses, the central figure through whom God gave the law to Israel. Earlier in the Gospel of John, Jesus is compared with Moses, who gave the law, while Jesus brought grace and truth ({{John 1:17|1:17}}; see also {{John 6:14-15|6:14–15}}). The Jewish leaders failed to accept the words of Moses, who spoke clearly about the coming Messiah, including the promise of a prophet like himself (for example, {{Deuteronomy 18:15|Deuteronomy 18:15}}).

Jesus feeding the 5,000 recalls the Old Testament story of manna (bread from heaven) when Israel was in the wilderness ({{Exodus 16:1-36|Exodus 16}}). In that story, God provided bread each day for his people.

In the time of Jesus, some Jewish teachers believed that the Messiah would again give bread from heaven ({{Exodus 16:4|Exodus 16:4}}). They expected a new act of divine provision.

When Jesus fed the crowd, he met this expectation. However, he was not only giving physical bread. He was pointing to himself as the true bread from heaven, who gives life to the world.

Large crowds of people followed Jesus around as he travelled. They had seen Jesus heal people and they understood that he had power.

There were more than 5,000 hungry people sitting on the mountainside. Only one boy had any food. Jesus prayed over the boy’s fish and bread. Jesus turned it into more than enough food to feed the large crowd. After they had eaten there was a lot of food left over.

Everyone understood that the mighty work that Jesus had done was a sign. It was the fourth sign that John recorded. The crowd thought it meant that Jesus was the prophet they had been waiting for. Jesus avoided the crowd until he could teach them what the sign really meant.

Later that night he did a fifth sign that only his disciples saw. He walked towards the disciples over rough waters. Seeing Jesus do this scared his disciples. Jesus was showing them that he has power and control over the world God created. Jesus comforted the disciples and helped them reach the place where they were going to.
Each story in this chapter uses the setting of the Feast of the Passover ({{John 6:4|6:4}}) to communicate a deeper meaning.

*Where can we buy bread*: When the Israelites left Egypt after the first Passover and entered the desert, finding food and water was also their first concern ({{Exodus 15:22-16:3|Exodus 15:22–16:3}}).
Barley was a grain for poor people. The loaves were like pita bread. The two fish were likely salted. Together with the five barley loaves, they made one meal.

The count of about 5,000 included only the men, as was the usual way of counting in that culture ({{Matthew 14:21|Matthew 14:21}}). Including women and children, the total number of people was much greater.

The simple meal provided the crowd with as much as they wanted. This was similar to the miracle of manna in the wilderness ({{Exodus 16:35|Exodus 16:35}}). In that earlier story, God gave bread from heaven through Moses. Now, Jesus provided bread for the people in a similar way.

*Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world*: The crowd understood the miracle as a fulfillment of Old Testament promises (see {{Deuteronomy 18:15|Deuteronomy 18:15}}, {{Deuteronomy 18:18|18}}; {{Malachi 4:5-6|Malachi 4:5–6}}).
*they were about to come and make Him king by force*: To avoid this role, Jesus fled the crowd and commanded his disciples to go back across the lake ({{Mark 6:45-46|Mark 6:45–46}}).

Strong east-west winds often blow down from the eastern cliffs of the Sea of Galilee. These winds usually come late in the day.

When the wind rushes down toward the water, it can quickly stir up high waves. As a result, the lake can become very rough and dangerous. Sudden and violent storms were common in that area.

The disciples were afraid of the storm. Then they saw Jesus walking on the water toward them. At that moment, their fear of the storm was replaced by fear and awe of him. Jesus came to help them. By walking on the water, he showed his authority over nature.

This act recalled Moses, who led Israel safely through the water ({{Exodus 14:1-31|Exodus 14}}; see {{Psalm 77:19-20|Psalm 77:19–20}}).
*It is I* (literally, *I am*): Jesus identified himself by the name God had revealed to Moses on Mount Sinai (see {{Exodus 3:14|Exodus 3:14}}; also see {{John 4:26|John 4:26}}; {{John 6:35|6:35}}).
*at once the boat reached the shore where they were heading*: The healing happened at once. This immediate result was another miracle performed by Jesus.

The crowd that had been fed kept looking for Jesus. They found him in Capernaum and asked him many questions.

Jesus had given them bread on the mountainside. Now he taught them about spiritual bread and food. People’s bodies need food to stay alive. To be alive spiritually people need the spiritual food that Jesus gives. People receive this spiritual food by believing that God sent Jesus and by following him. This is like eating spiritual bread.

God had given the Israelites manna through Moses. It took away their hunger for a little while. That bread didn’t make them live for ever. God sent Jesus as the spiritual bread for all people to eat. It allows them to live for ever.

Jesus said I am the bread of life. This was the first of Jesus’ seven I am statements recorded by John. It was hard for people to understand what Jesus was talking about. He was inviting them to believe that he is God’s Son. Those who believe this and follow Jesus will be raised from the dead. They will have eternal life and live with God for ever.
The crowd sailed north to Capernaum to search for Jesus because he had made Capernaum his home in Galilee ({{Mark 2:1|Mark 2:1}}).

The crowd had decided that Jesus was a prophet. They even wanted to use him for their own political goals (see {{John 6:15|6:15}}). 

However, they did not understand the true meaning of the miracle. They focused on the bread and the signs.

Jesus then explained what the miracle really meant. He taught that people should not work only for food that spoils. Instead, they should seek the food that gives eternal life ({{John 6:27-59|6:27–59}}).

This dialogue took place in the synagogue at Capernaum shortly before Passover ({{John 6:59|6:}}{{John 6:4|4,}}{{John 6:59|59}}). During Passover, Jews would read the story of the exodus from Egypt (see {{Exodus 1:1-15:27|Exodus 1–15}}).

The greatest gift Jesus gives is not physical bread, but eternal life. The Father gave Jesus the authority to do this. 

Physical food spoils. But Jesus, who is the bread of life, offers a gift that lasts forever ({{John 6:35|6:35}}).

The crowd asked Jesus for another miraculous sign. They wanted proof that he was the Messiah.

Many Jews believed that when the Messiah came, he would repeat the great miracle connected with Moses. They expected manna to fall from heaven again, as it had in the wilderness.

If that happened, people would see it as a second exodus. It would remind them of how God rescued Israel from Egypt and fed them in the desert.

Jesus corrected the people's argument: God, not Moses, fed Israel in the wilderness. 

The most important goal in life is to seek the true bread from God. This bread is not ordinary food. It is the gift that gives eternal life. To “eat” this bread means to believe in Jesus and depend on him.

Those who receive this bread share in the life that comes from God and lasts forever.
*Sir, … give us this bread*: This is similar to the request of the Samaritan woman ({{John 4:15|4:15}}). Spiritual awakening begins with a request for God’s gift.

- In the Gospel of John, the “I am” statements reveal who Jesus is and what he came to do (see also {{John 4:26|4:26}}; {{John 8:12|8:12}}; {{John 9:5|9:5}}; {{John 10:7-9|10:7–9}}, {{John 10:11-14|11–14}}; {{John 11:25|11:25}}; {{John 14:6|14:6}}; {{John 15:1-5|15:1–5}}). Jesus used the words *I am* on purpose. These words would remind his listeners of the name of God in the Old Testament ({{Exodus 3:14|Exodus 3:14}}). 

- *I am the bread of life*: Jesus is the true manna that came from God ({{John 6:38|John 6:38}}). He satisfies the spiritual hunger of those who believe in him (compare {{John 4:10-13|4:10–13}}).
*Everyone the Father gives Me*: God acts to bring people to Jesus so that they believe in him.

The mission of Jesus is sure to succeed. God sent Jesus and calls people to follow him ({{John 6:37|6:37,}}{{John 6:38|38,}}{{John 6:44|44}}). Those who come to him are secure in the promise Jesus gave that he will not reject them or lose them ({{John 6:39|6:39}}).

- When Jesus called himself *the bread that came down from heaven*, the crowd had to make a decision. 

- *Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph*: The people questioned Jesus because they thought they knew him and his family.

Their familiarity with him made his claims seem strange and unbelievable. Since they saw him as an ordinary man from their town, they struggled to accept what he said about himself.

*Stop grumbling*: Instead of defending himself against their complaint, Jesus addresses their lack of spiritual receptivity (their openness to God; see {{John 6:42|6:42}}). Those who love the Father and listen to him will believe in Jesus.

Jesus connected the manna of the exodus story with himself. Then he said why he was different from the manna the Israelites received from God. 

The Israelites remained mortal and they all died. But the bread from heaven (Jesus himself) provides eternal life ({{John 6:47|6:47}}, {{John 6:51|51}}, {{John 6:58|58}}).
*this bread … is My flesh*: The gift that gives life is now made clear. On the cross, Jesus gave his body so that the world might receive life.

*eats My flesh and drinks My blood*: Jesus answered the question the people asked ({{John 6:52|6:52}}). His words pointed ahead to the Lord’s Supper, which would come later (see {{Luke 22:19|Luke 22:19}}). In Jewish speech, the phrase “flesh and blood” referred to the whole person. In this context, Jesus was calling people to receive him fully by completely believing in him.

Ever since the Protestant Reformation, there have been three main interpretations of the words of Jesus about the bread and wine: 

- Transubstantiation: The bread and wine are believed to change into the actual body and blood of Christ, while still appearing to be bread and wine.

- Real Presence: Christ is understood to be truly present in the sacrament in a mysterious but real way that is beyond human understanding.

- Memorial or Symbolic View: The bread and wine are seen as symbols. The act of sharing them recalls Christ’s death and resurrection, and believers receive spiritual benefit through faith.

What Jesus said was shocking and offensive ({{John 6:53-58|6:53–58}}; see {{Genesis 9:4-5|Genesis 9:4–5}}). It was hard for his disciples and the crowd to understand. Should they take him literally? How could they eat his flesh? Jesus answers in {{John 6:63|John 6:63}}.

The people of Israel were excited about Jesus and the mighty works he did. But the spiritual truths he taught were hard to understand. The people didn’t know how to obey them. They were hard even for Jesus’ disciples.

Many disciples stopped following Jesus because they couldn’t accept his words. Jesus asked his 12 closest disciples if they would also leave him. Simon Peter spoke for the whole group and showed that they were committed to Jesus.

Peter was the third witness in John’s gospel to say who Jesus is. He called Jesus the Holy One of God. This was a way of saying that Jesus is Israel’s King and Messiah. Yet one of the 12 disciples wouldn’t remain faithful to Jesus.

The true source of the gift Jesus gives is the Holy Spirit, not human effort. In this context,* the flesh* refers to what humans can do on their own. Life and understanding come through the gift of the Spirit (see {{John 14:15-20|14:15–20}}; {{John 20:21-22|20:21–22}}). True life is found only when the Holy Spirit gives life to people.
*no one can come to Me unless the Father has granted it to him* (see {{John 6:44|6:44}}): Only God’s light can shine into the deep darkness of the world.

Simon Peter often spoke on behalf of the 12 apostles (see also {{Matthew 14:28-29|Matthew 14:28–29}}; {{Matthew 16:16|16:16}}; {{Matthew 17:4|17:4}}; {{Matthew 18:21|18:21}}; {{Matthew 19:27|19:27}}; {{Matthew 26:33-35|26:33–35}}).

- Once again, Jesus showed supernatural knowledge (knowledge beyond normal human ability; see {{John 1:47-49|1:47–49}}; {{John 4:16-19|4:16–19}}). He knew what was in people’s hearts (their innermost selves) and what would happen in the future.

Jesus knew that Judas would betray him. Judas later betrayed Jesus to the authorities ({{John 12:4|12:4}}; {{John 13:2|13:2}}; {{Matthew 26:14-16|Matthew 26:14–16}}). 

- *Iscariot* means “man from Kerioth.” Kerioth was the home village of Judas’s family.

The Jewish leaders from Jerusalem and Judea didn’t believe that God sent Jesus. They wanted him to be killed.

Jesus’ brothers didn’t believe what Jesus said about himself either. They thought that Jesus just wanted fame and glory for himself.

The crowds at the Feast of Booths in Jerusalem had many different opinions about Jesus. He wasn’t what they thought the messiah would be like. No one understood how Jesus knew all the things he taught about.

Jesus explained to them again that everything he did and taught came from God. He talked about when he had healed the man on the Sabbath day. He wanted people to judge his actions based on the work God did through him. They shouldn’t judge him based on their rules.

Jesus talked about how he would soon return to his Father. The religious leaders thought he was talking about going away somewhere. They sent guards to arrest him but Jesus wasn’t afraid. He didn’t stop working or teaching.

This chapter describes Jesus at the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles. Jesus used parts of the feast to reveal his true identity to his fellow Jews and to show that he had fulfilled the feast's essential meaning (see {{John 7:37-39|7:37–39}}; {{John 8:12|8:12}}).

The law of Moses required Jewish men to come to the temple for the Feast of Tabernacles ({{Exodus 23:14-17|Exodus 23:14–17}}; {{Deuteronomy 16:16|Deuteronomy 16:16}}). This annual seven-day autumn harvest feast happened in Jerusalem six months after Passover ({{John 6:4|John 6:4}}). 

During the feast, people lived in temporary shelters to remember the tents Israel used during their 40 years in the wilderness.

The brothers of Jesus reminded him of his religious duty to go to the festival (see also {{Mark 3:31|Mark 3:31}}). Their words carried a cynical tone because at this time they did not believe in him ({{John 7:5|John 7:5}}).

*My time has not yet come*: Jesus said that it was not the right time for him to go publicly to Jerusalem.

Later, however, he did go to the city. He went quietly and not in a public way ({{John 7:10|7:10}}; compare study note on 12:23).

They wondered how he could teach with such understanding.

Jesus had not studied under a well-known rabbi (a Jewish teacher of the law). Instead, he said that his teaching came from his heavenly Father.

This was different from many Jewish teachers. For example, Peter and John were known as untrained men ({{Acts 4:13|Acts 4:13}}). In contrast, Paul had studied under a respected teacher ({{Acts 22:3|Acts 22:3}}).

People who truly want to follow God's will accept Jesus and his teachings (see also {{John 5:42-47|5:42–47}}). 

In contrast, those who focus only on the values and desires of this world are not open to Christ. When people care more about human approval, power, or temporary success, they struggle to receive his message.

*Has not Moses given you the law? Yet not one of you keeps it*: The Jewish leaders were proud of the law of Moses. They believed they carefully obeyed it.

However, Jesus pointed out a serious problem. While they honored the law in words, they were planning to kill him. In doing so, they were breaking the law ({{Exodus 20:13|Exodus 20:13}}).

The law required circumcision on the eighth day ({{Leviticus 12:3|Leviticus 12:3}}). It allowed a boy to be circumcised even if that day was the Sabbath. 

Jesus argued in the way many rabbis did. They reasoned from the lesser to the greater. If a smaller religious act, such as circumcision, was allowed on the Sabbath, then a greater act, such as making a whole person well, should also be allowed.

Some people in the crowd believed they knew where Jesus came from. Because they could trace his earthly origins, they thought he could not be the Messiah.

They expected the Messiah to appear suddenly and in a mysterious way. Since Jesus had grown up among them, they assumed he did not fit their expectations.

*I am from Him*: Instead of answering questions about where he grew up ({{John 7:27|7:27}}, {{John 7:40-44|40–44}}), Jesus spoke about where he truly came from. He pointed to his heavenly origin.

He said that he was sent by God. This was a bold claim.

The religious leaders understood what he meant. Because of this, they tried to arrest him. They believed he was speaking in a way that dishonored God ({{John 7:30|7:30}}; compare {{John 10:30-33|10:30–33}}).

*His hour had not yet come*: Those who opposed Jesus could not arrest him. This was because, according to God's plan, the time for Jesus to be glorified on the cross had not yet come (see study note on 12:23; see also {{John 10:17-18|10:17–18}}; {{John 18:6-8|18:6–8}}). 

All four arrest scenes in {{John 7:1-8:59|7:1–8:59}} emphasize that Jesus was in control, not the Jewish leaders.

- Jesus announced his return to the one who sent him, the Father in heaven ({{John 17:1-7|17:1–7}}). But the Pharisees misunderstood him. They thought he was leaving Judea to visit the Gentiles (non-Jewish people). These were people whom Pharisees would never visit. 

- After Jesus returned to the Father, the Jewish leaders would no longer be able to find him.

- *and where I am, you cannot come*: These Pharisees, still in spiritual darkness, could not enter heaven. So Jesus would be beyond their reach there.

- *Living water*: See {{John 4:10-14|4:10–14}}. A water ceremony was held each day during the Feast of Tabernacles, with prayer for God to send rain in the late autumn. 

The final day, called *the great day*, was the feast's most important moment. On this day, they repeated the ceremony seven times. They poured water over the altar while Levites sang {{Isaiah 12:3|Isaiah 12:3}} (see {{Zechariah 14:8|Zechariah 14:8}}; see also *Mishnah Sukkah* chapter 4). 

- *If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink*: Jesus fulfilled an important part of the Feast of Tabernacles. He himself is the source of living water, available to anyone who believes.

Water was an important part of the Feast of Booths. On the last day of the feast Jesus talked about water in a spiritual way. Jesus claimed that the water of new life comes from him. Those who believe he is God’s Son will have this living water. It will flow from inside them like rivers.

Jesus was talking about the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit would be given to all who trust and believe in Jesus. The people at the feast wondered how this could be. They couldn’t agree about who Jesus was. But almost all the religious leaders agreed that he was trying to trick people.

Nicodemus wanted the leaders to try to understand Jesus. But they weren’t open to hearing anything Jesus had to say.

In the death and resurrection of Jesus, his life was given for others, and the Holy Spirit was given to believers.

When Jesus was crucified, blood and water flowed from his side (see {{John 19:34|19:34}}). This event points to the gift of life that comes through his death.

After he rose from the dead, he breathed on his disciples and gave them the Holy Spirit ({{John 20:22|20:22}}). In this way, his life and the Spirit were poured out for his followers.

These Jews were not like the crowd who thought the Christ (the Messiah) would have a mysterious appearance ({{John 7:25-27|7:25–27}}). They believed the prophecy that God's chosen ruler would come from Bethlehem in Judea (see {{Micah 5:2|Micah 5:2}}). However, they struggled with the fact that Jesus seemed to be from Galilee, where he grew up.

- The story ends with Jewish leaders feeling frustrated and the people being divided over their opinion of Jesus (compare {{John 7:25-27|7:25–27}}, {{John 7:31-32|31–32}}). 

- *officers returned*: See {{John 7:32|7:32}}.

Nicodemus was likely starting to believe in Jesus (see {{John 3:1-21|3:1–21}}; {{John 19:38-42|19:38–42}}). Some leaders claimed that none of the Pharisees believed in Jesus ({{John 7:48|7:48}}). They spoke as if only the crowd, whom the leaders believed did not understand the law, supported him.

However, Nicodemus shows that this was not completely true. Not only the people in the crowd, but also some Pharisees were beginning to believe in him.

*no prophet comes out of Galilee*: The Jewish leaders were apparently unaware that Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea, not in Galilee (see {{Matthew 2:1|Matthew 2:1}}; {{Luke 2:1-7|Luke 2:1–7}}).
It is likely that someone added this story to John's Gospel later, since it is not in the earliest Greek manuscripts. However, it is likely a true story from the life of Jesus.

The Law of Moses said that people mustn’t commit adultery. Both the man and the woman who were guilty of adultery had to be put to death.

The Pharisees caught a woman committing adultery. This meant that they would have caught the man at the same time. But they never brought the man to Jesus.

The leaders weren’t really interested in the two people or what they did. They wanted to trap Jesus into doing or saying something against the Law of Moses. But Jesus didn’t speak against the Law as they had hoped he would. Instead, he showed them that they were also guilty of sin.

Jesus didn’t judge the woman as guilty. He told her to stop sinning and to live in a way that honoured God.
*The scribes and Pharisees*: The teachers of religious law were Jewish scholars. They specialized in the Old Testament law and oral traditions that explained it.

The form of the Greek sentence emphasizes the legal claim against the woman. She had been caught while committing the sin of adultery. The law required two witnesses and carefully outlined what evidence was needed.

- *In the Law Moses commanded us to stone*: This suggests the woman was engaged or married ({{Leviticus 20:10|Leviticus 20:10}}; {{Deuteronomy 22:23-24|Deuteronomy 22:23–24}}). The law also indicates that the man who sinned with her must die as well. But these Jewish religious leaders ignored that part of the law. 

- They could have dealt with the situation privately to avoid shaming her. But their real intention was to condemn Jesus instead. They asked him, *So what do you say?* 

Would he neglect the law since he had a reputation for mercy? Or would he ignore the woman’s tragedy?
We cannot know what Jesus wrote in the dust. Some scholars suggest he wrote down the sins of those who were accusing the woman.

The answer Jesus gave did not mean that someone who makes an accusation must be morally perfect to make legal claims. He referred to *him who is without sin* to point to the motives of those accusing her.
*they began to go away one by one*: One of the people accusing her left, then another, followed by several people who had been standing there watching what was happening.

*neither do I*: Jesus spoke words of assurance, but this did not suggest that the woman was innocent. Jesus takes sin and judgment seriously, but he shows grace and forgiveness to those overcome by sin.

During the Festival of Tabernacles, people filled 16 gold bowls in the temple's inner courts with oil and lit them. Jesus stood under these lights in the temple and said that he was now the source of the light of the world ({{John 8:20|8:20}}). The light of Jesus brings salvation to both Israel and the world, regardless of race or location.

Jesus said I am the Light of the world. This was the second I am statement in John’s gospel. This was a bold claim.

Jesus is the Light that God wants to share with the whole world. John had said this at the beginning of his gospel.

The religious leaders held what was like a trial to decide who Jesus is. Jesus and the leaders talked about witnesses, about judging and about truth.

Jesus’ main point was that he spoke and shared what the Father told him to. The words he spoke were the Father’s words.

Jesus showed who the Father is in a clear and direct way. Some people believed Jesus when they heard the claims that he made.

The debate about whether Jesus is the Messiah continues from {{John 7:52|7:52}}. Jesus remained at the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem. During the feast, the conflicts Jesus encountered in chapter {{John 7:1-53|7}} continued and intensified.

The Pharisees argued that what Jesus was saying about himself was not valid because Jewish law requires more than one witness ({{Deuteronomy 19:15|Deuteronomy 19:15}}; compare {{John 5:31-32|John 5:31–32}}; see {{John 8:17|8:17}}).

Jesus responded to the Pharisees' accusations. He said he could make these claims about himself because he knew both his origin and his destination were heaven. He then said the most important witness for his case was his Father who sent him ({{John 8:16|8:16}}).

Throughout the feast, those listening to Jesus proved they were in darkness as they misunderstood him. They wanted to meet the father of Jesus, who is God. Since they did not truly know God, they were unable to understand Jesus.
