- The treasury was in the section of the temple called the Court of the Women. Jesus often taught there so both men and women could listen ({{Mark 12:41|Mark 12:41}}). 

- *His hour*: See notes on {{John 2:4|John 2:4}}; {{John 12:23|12:23}}.

In the earlier debate at the feast, people questioned where Jesus came from ({{John 7:27|7:27}}). Here, Jesus talked about returning to where he came from (heaven). However, once again, his words were misunderstood by the people listening.

Jesus told his listeners that they were *from below,* while he was *from above *({{John 3:31|3:31}}; see study note on 3:3).

*From below* refers to human life limited to this world. *From above* refers to heaven and to God’s realm.

Because they were thinking only in earthly terms, they could not understand what Jesus meant. His origin and authority came from God.

- *unless you believe that I am He*: Jesus used God's divine name (see {{John 4:26|4:26}}; {{Exodus 3:14|Exodus 3:14}}). His listeners did not fully understand the meaning of his words ({{John 8:25|John 8:25}}). 

- *die in your sins*: Jesus is the light who has come into the world. His presence offers the only way of salvation. If people reject him, they remain in darkness and do not receive life.
*Who are you?*: Later, they understood what he was claiming about himself. They believed he was showing dishonor toward God. Because of this, they tried to stone him ({{John 8:59|8:59}}).

The Synoptic Gospels describe Jesus as predicting his death three times (for example, {{Mark 8:31|Mark 8:31}}; {{Mark 9:31|9:31}}; {{Mark 10:33-34|10:33–34}}). 

The Gospel of John presents this theme in a different way. Jesus speaks about being *lifted up* ({{John 3:14|John 3:14}}; {{John 8:28|8:28}}; {{John 12:33-34|12:33–34}}). This phrase refers to his crucifixion and also to his glory. The Father directs the course of events. The death of Jesus did not happen by accident, but according to God’s plan.

Once again, the crowd at the feast was divided. Earlier, the discussion had ended with plans to arrest Jesus ({{John 8:20|8:20}}). Now many people believed in him. They were persuaded that he was speaking the truth.

However, when Jesus spoke more clearly about who he really was, their faith was tested. As his full identity became known, some struggled to accept his words ({{John 8:31-59|8:31–59}}).

- Discipleship involves more than just knowing who Jesus is. It also requires obeying his teachings ({{John 3:36|3:36}}; {{John 14:15|14:15}}, {{John 14:21|21}}, {{John 14:23|23}}; {{John 15:10|15:10}}). 

- Because Jesus is the truth, knowing him helps a person understand what is true and what is false ({{John 14:6|14:6}}).

- *set you free*: The truth frees a person from darkness, lies, and sin.

Jesus said that those who obey him understand the truth about who he is. This truth sets people free.

The religious leaders argued that they were already free. They were sure of their own family line and that they weren’t slaves. But Jesus explained that they were slaves to sin. Sin kept them from being fully part of God’s family.

Jesus could set them free from their sin and make them part of God’s family. He could do this because he is the Son in God’s family.

The leaders claimed they were already in God’s family because Abraham was their father. They said that God was their Father too. But Jesus said that they didn’t act like Abraham or do what God wanted. When Abraham heard from God, he believed God and obeyed God’s words. But the religious leaders refused to believe God’s words through Jesus and didn’t obey him.

By not obeying the truth, they were acting like the devil. Jesus said that those who obey him would never die. He was talking about when God will raise them from the dead. That is when God will give them eternal life.

Jesus spoke about himself as I am. This was a way for Jesus to tell people that he is God. This made the Jewish leaders so angry that they tried to kill him.

- Jesus challenged a common belief about Israel as God’s chosen people. Many thought that being descendants of Abraham gave them special privilege and protection.

Instead of seeing this heritage as a responsibility to obey God, some treated it as a guarantee of safety. However, the prophets had warned that privilege brings accountability (compare {{Amos 3:1-15|Amos 3:1–15}}). 

- The people did not understand what Jesus meant by *set free*. He was not talking about freedom from human slavery. He meant freedom from spiritual slavery to sin ({{John 8:34|John 8:34}}). 

True freedom comes through the truth. It does not come from family history or religious background ({{John 8:32|8:32}}; {{Romans 6:17|Romans 6:17}}; {{Romans 8:2|8:2}}; {{1 John 3:4|1 John 3:4}}, {{1 John 3:8|8}}, {{1 John 3:9|9}}).

Jesus explained his argument: If Israel is a spiritual slave, it has the same insecurity as any slave in a household. Family members are secure, but slaves are not. Only Jesus can change the status of those in spiritual slavery, making them free and secure.

The leaders' plan to kill Jesus revealed their true identity ({{John 5:18|5:18}}). They were part of a different spiritual family, and their spiritual father was not Jesus's Father. They were relying on the fact that their ancestral father was Abraham, but Jesus challenged their spiritual heritage. 

The most important part of his challenge comes in {{John 8:44|8:44}}.

- *your father*: Jesus knew who controlled them. 

- *We are not illegitimate children*: This statement acted as both a defense and an attack. The Greek text emphasizes the pronoun *we*. In other words, “*We* [in contrast to *you*] *are not illegitimate.*” They are suggesting that Jesus was illegitimate (see {{Matthew 1:18-25|Matthew 1:18–25}}).

Since the unbelieving people did not love Jesus ({{John 8:42|8:42}}; {{1 John 5:1|1 John 5:1}}), they were not children of the Father in heaven who sent his beloved Son ({{John 8:47|John 8:47}}). Their desire to kill God’s Son showed their true spiritual heritage. This was the work of the devil, who brought death to the world (see {{Genesis 3:1-20|Genesis 3:1–20}}; {{Romans 5:12-14|Romans 5:12–14}}).

By calling Jesus a Samaritan with a demon, his opponents used a racial insult to dismiss his accusations (see study note on 4:4–6). They claimed Jesus was demon-possessed to counter his claim that they belonged to Satan (also {{John 7:20|7:20}}; {{John 8:52|8:52}}; {{John 10:20|10:20}}; {{John 8:44|8:44}}). 

Jesus rightly replied that these words were deeply offensive. In fact, it was a serious and unforgivable offense ({{Mark 3:22-29|Mark 3:22–29}}).

*Who do You claim to be?*: This question was hostile and aggressive. However, if Jesus is immortal, ruling over life and death, then he is greater than Abraham, the prophets, or any of the greatest people in Israel’s history ({{John 8:58|8:58}}).
Like his opponents, Jesus appealed to Abraham. Rabbis taught that God had given Abraham prophetic insight, teaching him about the coming age of the Messiah.

*You are not yet fifty years old*: The Jewish leaders misunderstood Jesus. Jesus was not talking about his physical age. He was speaking about his divine pre-existence (his existence before he was born as a human).

- *before Abraham was born, I am!: *The life of Jesus spans the past from before creation and continues forever ({{John 1:1-2|1:1–2}}). 

- *I am*: This title recalls the name of God revealed to Moses at Mount Sinai ({{Exodus 3:14|Exodus 3:14}}; compare {{John 4:26|John 4:26}}; {{Isaiah 43:11-13|Isaiah 43:11–13}}; {{Isaiah 48:12|48:12}}).

- Those listening to Jesus finally understood his claim to be God ({{John 8:58|8:58}}). Because of this, they became very angry. They believed they had heard blasphemy (words that dishonored God) and picked up stones to throw at him, which was the proper legal response ({{Leviticus 24:16|Leviticus 24:16}}). 

- Jesus was hidden from them because God had chosen a different time for his death (see study note on John 12:23; see also {{John 7:30|7:30}}, {{John 7:44|44}}; {{Luke 4:29-30|Luke 4:29–30}}).

After seeing a blind man, the disciples tried to understand illness and suffering. Was it a punishment for someone’s sin?

Jesus answered that the man wasn’t born blind because someone did something wrong. In fact, Jesus would use the man’s illness to show God’s power. He healed the blind man.

This was Jesus’ sixth sign in John’s gospel. Healing people was part of the work God had sent Jesus to do. Jesus is God’s Light. He would do God’s works as long as he was in the world.

Everyone who had known the man before was shocked. It was hard to believe that the man who had been blind could now see.

At the Feast of Tabernacles, Jesus claimed to be the light of the world (chapters {{John 7:1-8:59|7–8}}; see {{John 8:12|8:12}}). Now John tells about Jesus giving light, both physically and spiritually, to a blind man who lived in darkness (see {{John 9:5|9:5}}). 

The story ends with a surprising reversal (a complete change) of roles: The man who had been blind was assumed to live in spiritual darkness. Yet he came to see and accept God’s light. The Pharisees could see with their physical eyes. People thought they were spiritually enlightened (well taught and wise). However, they refused to believe. In the end, they were shown to be spiritually blind.
The disciples thought the man was born blind because of sin, either his own sin or his parents'. Jesus corrected this common belief ({{John 9:3|9:3}}).
*I am the light of the world*: See study note on 8:12.
During the New Testament era, saliva was used for medical purposes (see {{Mark 7:32-35|Mark 7:32–35}}; {{Mark 8:22-25|8:22–25}}).

- Siloam, a pool at the south end of Jerusalem, provided water for the Feast of Tabernacles ceremonies. 

- *which means “Sent”*: This phrase contained a double meaning: Jesus, who has been *sent* by God, told the blind man to wash in the pool called *Sent* ({{John 4:34|4:34}}; {{John 5:23|5:23}}, {{John 5:37|37}}; {{John 7:28|7:28}}; {{John 8:26|8:26}}; {{John 12:44|12:44}}; {{John 14:24|14:24}}).

The blind man recognized Jesus and spoke with confidence about him. Jesus healed the man of his physical problem, and the man gained more spiritual understanding ({{John 9:17|9:17}}, {{John 9:33|33}}). He became a disciple of Jesus ({{John 9:38|9:38}}; compare {{John 5:11-15|5:11–15}}).

The Pharisees were experts in interpreting the Jewish law. So the community asked them to explain this miracle (see {{John 1:24|1:24}}). Instead of celebrating the healing, these religious leaders questioned the man because Jesus had performed the miracle on the Sabbath (see {{John 5:16-18|5:16–18}}).

Once again there was conflict with the religious leaders. They understood the Law of Moses in a certain way. Jesus understood it in a different way.

Jesus had healed people on the Sabbath day before. He had already explained that this didn’t break the Law of Moses. The Pharisees couldn’t agree with one another. Some only cared about Jesus breaking the rules. Others saw proof of God’s power in the signs that Jesus did.

This story is filled with things that are the opposite of what is expected. A man who had been blind since birth could see. The Pharisees saw with their eyes but were blind to spiritual truth. They claimed to know many things but couldn’t understand how Jesus healed a man.

A humble man with no training knew what had happened to him and who made it happen. He spoke clearly while the Pharisees remained confused. The blind man was the one teaching the religious leaders about the ways of God. They were unkind to him and threw him out of the synagogue.
The man had already identified his healer ({{John 9:11|9:11}}, {{John 9:16|16}}). Now he made his own spiritual judgment, calling Jesus a prophet.

The Pharisees wanted to dismiss the miracle. They did not want to accept that Jesus had truly healed the man.

They called the man’s parents and questioned them. They hoped the parents would deny that a real healing had taken place.
His parents confirmed that their son had been born blind, but they hesitated to judge how he could see because they were afraid of the social consequences.

- The Pharisees could not argue against the logic of the miracle ({{John 9:24-25|9:24–25}}, {{John 9:30-33|30–33}}). So they abandoned reason and cursed him (see {{John 9:34|9:34}}). 

- The harsh division between Jesus and the religious leaders was clear. They considered those who followed Jesus to have rejected Moses and Judaism.

The Jewish leaders did not know where Jesus came from. It made sense that the man was amazed. A healing like this had never happened before. 

The work of Jesus showed he was from God. Once people knew who he truly was, they should have believed and followed him. However, the Jewish leaders chose to ignore the truth.

Only God could give sight to someone born blind. By healing the man, Jesus gave the Jewish leaders an obvious sign that he was from God and was the Messiah (compare {{Psalm 146:8|Psalm 146:8}}; {{Isaiah 35:5|Isaiah 35:5}}; {{Isaiah 42:7|42:7}}).

Discipline such as being thrown out of the synagogue was not uncommon. It brought social isolation that might require the man’s departure from the village. Such serious persecution was precisely what Jesus predicted for his followers ({{John 15:18-27|15:18–27}}; {{John 16:2|16:2}}).

*Son of Man*: See {{John 1:51|1:51}}; {{John 3:13|3:13}}, {{John 3:14|14}}; {{John 5:27|5:27}}; {{John 6:27|6:27}}, {{John 6:53|53}}, {{John 6:62|62}}; {{John 8:28|8:28}}. The Greek expression translates a Hebrew and Aramaic phrase that means *human being*. People were often unsure what Jesus meant when he used this title (see {{John 12:34|12:34}}). In {{Daniel 7:13-14|Daniel 7:13–14}}, a human figure receives authority and an eternal kingdom from God. Later Jewish tradition connected this figure with hopes for the Messiah. John uses the title *Son of Man* to point to Jesus as both an ordinary human being and the Messiah appointed by God.

Jesus urged the man who had been blind to understand the miracle and recognize the one who healed him. The man immediately showed faith and honored Jesus in the same way he would honor God ({{John 9:38|9:38}}; compare {{John 20:28|20:28}}).

Jesus searched for the man he had healed. That man wasn’t allowed to worship God in the synagogue any longer. When Jesus found him, the man worshipped Jesus.

Jesus talked about people being like sheep and himself as a shepherd. Jesus was a good shepherd to the man he healed. The blind man was like the sheep who heard the shepherd’s voice and followed him.

Jesus described the sheep pen like a shelter for God’s family. People enter the sheep pen through Jesus. That is why Jesus said I am like a gate for the sheep. This was one of his I am statements. Another one was when Jesus said, I am the good shepherd.

Other leaders were like hired workers or even like thieves and robbers. But Jesus knows each sheep by name and loves each one. He wants all people to be joined together like sheep in one sheep pen. They will know the Father and will have everything they need. Jesus gave his life so that his sheep could live in the fullest possible way.

*Are we blind too?*: Jesus answered that those who claim to hold all religious truth will discover that they are blind, while those who recognize their spiritual poverty will find true sight. In the story, the blind man and his family frequently confessed that they did not know, while the Pharisees repeatedly stated their confidence and remained guilty because of their religious pride. If they had confessed their ignorance and admitted their spiritual blindness, they would be guiltless. Instead, their conscious and willful rejection of Jesus established their guilt.

- A shepherd in the wild would build a sheepfold. This was a pen with low stone walls topped by sharp branches, to keep his sheep safe at night. 

- The pen had one gate (or opening in the wall) that was closed with branches. Any person or thing that came into the pen threatened the flock. 

- A bad shepherd was like *a thief and a robber*. He used the sheep for his own gain and did not care for them. Bad shepherds took the sheep’s milk and wool for themselves. They killed the sheep without guaranteeing their safety ({{Ezekiel 34:3|Ezekiel 34:3}}; see {{Isaiah 56:11|Isaiah 56:11}}; {{Jeremiah 23:1-4|Jeremiah 23:1–4}}). 

These words were the strongest rebuke Jesus spoke against the Jewish leaders.

This illustration of a shepherd and his sheep comes from a Middle Eastern perspective of shepherding and Old Testament traditions in first-century AD Jewish culture. God was the shepherd of Israel ({{Genesis 49:24|Genesis 49:24}}; {{Psalm 23:1-6|Psalms 23}}; {{Psalm 78:52-53|78:52–53}}; {{Isaiah 40:10-11|Isaiah 40:10–11}}). 

Spiritual and political leaders of Israel were also shepherds of God’s people, the flock of God ({{Isaiah 56:9-12|Isaiah 56:9–12}}; {{Jeremiah 23:1-4|Jeremiah 23:1–4}}; {{Ezekiel 34:1-31|Ezekiel 34}}). 

Jesus spoke these words during the Feast of Dedication (see {{John 10:22|John 10:22}}). At that time, people remembered both faithful and unfaithful leaders in Israel’s history.

In this setting, Jesus addressed the theme of shepherds. He spoke in a way that echoes {{Ezekiel 34:1-31|Ezekiel 34}}, where God condemns bad shepherds and promises to care for his people himself. Jesus then identified himself as the good shepherd ({{John 10:11-14|John 10:11–14}}).

{{John 10:1-42|Chapter 10}} continues the series of feast sermons (see study note on 5:1–10:42). Here, the setting is the Feast of Dedication. The timing of this feast is important for understanding the story (see study note on 10:22).
*the sheep listen for his voice*: The Middle Eastern shepherd is well known for having intimate knowledge of the sheep. Sheep are led with flute tunes, songs, or verbal commands.
A good shepherd goes ahead of the sheep and leads them. He does not force them from behind. When the sheep recognize his voice, they trust him and follow.
I am: See study note on 6:35. A good shepherd protects the sheep at the gate like a guard.
*he will be saved* (or *will find safety*): As the guard at the gate, Jesus protects his sheep from harm by keeping them safe inside the pen.

The followers of Jesus must be wary of bad shepherds who desire to *steal and kill and destroy*. When they told the story of the Feast of Dedication to the Jewish people, it reminded them of false religious leaders (see study note on 10:22). The failures of these leaders had led to the loss of God's temple in Jerusalem during the time of the Maccabean Revolt.

Small villages often created communal flocks and employed a hired hand to tend the sheep. However, an employee lacked the commitment of a true shepherd. The wilderness of Judea had many predators. When a wolf or other predators attacked, the hired hand would run rather than defend the sheep. Jesus will never do this; he will always stand between his sheep and danger.

*I am*: See study note on 6:35. The good shepherd guides his sheep, finds food and water, and locates paths in the wilderness (see {{Psalm 23:1-6|Psalm 23}}). The good shepherd stands between his sheep and danger ({{John 10:11|John 10:11}}). 

The Old Testament describes God as Israel’s shepherd ({{Psalm 23:1-6|Psalms 23}}; {{Psalm 80:1|80:1}}; {{Isaiah 40:10-11|Isaiah 40:10–11}}). The religious leaders of God’s people should care for their flock as God does ({{Ezekiel 34:23|Ezekiel 34:23}}). However, the leaders of Israel in the time of Jesus were not good shepherds.
*I give my life for the sheep*: Jesus was speaking about his coming death. He was referring to his crucifixion (his death on a cross; chapter {{John 19:1-42|19}}).

The Father and the Son have an intimate relationship. Jesus shares a similar relationship with his sheep (his followers) through the Holy Spirit ({{John 14:23-31|14:23–31}}; {{John 15:1-11|15:1–11}}).

*other sheep*: Jesus spoke about sheep who were not part of the present sheepfold. This refers to people outside Judaism who would later believe in him (see {{John 11:52|11:52}}). The followers of Jesus would not be divided by ethnic background. Jewish and Gentile believers from many cultures would become one flock. There would be one shepherd and one united people ({{John 17:20-23|17:20–23}}).

- *No one takes it from Me*: The death of the Son was voluntary. Jesus was not a helpless victim of events beyond his control. He chose to give his life freely in obedience and close relationship with the Father (see {{Acts 2:23-24|Acts 2:23–24}}). 

- The resurrection of Jesus was not an afterthought or a rescue from failure. God cannot be confined by death or a tomb. Because Jesus and the Father are one, Jesus possessed the authority to rise from death.

- Jesus divided his audience yet again (see also {{John 6:66-69|6:66–69}}; {{John 7:43|7:43}}; {{John 9:16|9:16}}). His words and actions led people to one of two responses: opposition or faith.

- *He is demon-possessed*: Compare {{John 7:20|7:20}}; {{John 8:48-49|8:48–49}}, {{John 8:52|52}}.

*the Feast of Dedication*: This winter feast is also known as Hanukkah. It celebrates the time when the Jews rededicated the temple after Antiochus IV (175–163 BC) defiled it in. Two hundred years before Jesus was born, Greek soldiers captured the Jerusalem Temple, stole its treasures, and made it unusable for worship. 

In the winter of 165–164 BC, a Jewish army led by Judas Maccabeus reclaimed the temple and rededicated it to the Lord. The Feast of Hanukkah ("*dedication*") celebrates this event (see *1 Maccabees* 3–4; *2 Maccabees* 8:1–10:8). 

During the feast, priests examined their commitment to service, using {{Ezekiel 34:1-31|Ezekiel 34}} as their main text for reflection (also {{Jeremiah 23:1-4|Jeremiah 23:1–4}}; {{Jeremiah 25:32-38|25:32–38}}; {{Zechariah 11:1-17|Zechariah 11}}). At this Hanukkah celebration, Jesus used the shepherd theme from {{Ezekiel 34:1-31|Ezekiel 34}} to show he was the good shepherd ({{John 10:11|John 10:11}}). He also showed how Israel’s current religious leaders were bad shepherds ({{John 10:10|10:10}}, {{John 10:12-13|12–13}}).

The Jewish leaders wanted Jesus to say plainly if he was the Messiah. Jesus didn’t answer the way they wanted him to. He said that the works he had done should be enough proof.

As God’s Son he did God’s work in the world. Jesus’ works were the fourth witness to who he is. The works showed that Jesus and the Father are one. Those who believe this are Jesus’ sheep. They are protected for ever in the shelter of God's hand.

The Jewish leaders were very angry at the way Jesus was talking. They tried to kill him. Jesus left Jerusalem and went back across the River Jordan. People there trusted the works that Jesus did and believed in him.

Large covered walkways with rows of columns stood around all four sides of the temple’s central courtyard. These structures are called colonnades.

Solomon’s Colonnade was on the east side. It provided shelter from wind and rain, especially during the winter months.

The people around Jesus might have been trying to understand, or they might have been hostile. In {{Luke 21:20|Luke 21:20}} and {{Hebrews 11:30|Hebrews 11:30}}, the same word describes how armies surrounded Jerusalem and Jericho before their destruction. In {{Acts 14:20|Acts 14:20}}, it refers to Paul's disciples gathering around him after he was injured.

Jesus had already provided the Jewish people and their religious leaders with sufficient proof that he is the Son of God. The problem was not lack of information, but their unwillingness to believe him.

In his final public statement in this Gospel, Jesus gave a clear and complete declaration about who he is ({{John 10:30|10:30}}). He spoke openly about his unity with the Father.

This statement brought his public teaching to a high point and made his identity unmistakable.

- As the good shepherd, Jesus would die for his sheep and protect them from all predators and thieves ({{John 10:1|10:1}}, {{John 10:8|8}}, {{John 10:11|11}}; see {{Ezekiel 34:22-23|Ezekiel 34:22–23}}). 

- The Father's power, shown through Jesus, keeps his sheep safe. No one can steal from Jesus those who trust in him. This is because no one is stronger than Jesus. Their security depends on Christ, not their own efforts. 

- The word translated as *snatch* suggests violence (as in {{John 6:15|John 6:15}}).

The Father and the Son are distinct persons, yet they share one purpose and one divine nature ({{John 1:1|1:1}}, {{John 1:14|14}}; {{John 14:9|14:9}}; {{John 20:28|20:28}}). They are not the same person. Yet they are united in will, authority, and being.

Because of this unity, Jesus has the power to protect God’s flock ({{John 10:28-29|10:28–29}}). His words are a strong statement about his divinity.

The people understood what Jesus meant and wanted to kill him (see {{John 10:33|10:33}}). The problem was not that Jesus performed good works, but that he claimed to be God (see {{John 6:42|6:42}}, {{John 6:60|60}}; {{John 7:29-30|7:29–30}}). Blasphemy (speaking in a way that dishonors God) was punishable by death under the law of Moses. The required punishment was stoning (see {{Leviticus 24:23|Leviticus 24:23}}; {{John 8:59|John 8:59}}).

*‘I have said you are gods’*: If the word *gods* could describe people other than the Lord, then Jesus was not breaking the law by referring to himself in this way. But Jesus is not just any son of God. Jesus is *the Son of God* who *the Father* sent into the world.
The miraculous works Jesus performed should help true believers know and understand that the full reality of God dwells in Jesus.
His revelation to the Jewish leaders now complete, Jesus went to the region beyond the Jordan River where John the Baptist had once worked and where Jesus was baptized.

*everything he said about this man was true*: See {{John 1:19-51|1:19–51}}; {{John 3:22-36|3:22–36}}. The fulfillment of John the Baptist’s predictions confirms both that he was a prophet and that what he said about Jesus was true.

This is a note of irony (an unexpected contrast). In Jerusalem, the holy city, Jesus found little faith among the religious leaders. But in the desert, away from the center of religious power, many people believed in him.

- In the Hebrew language, *Lazarus* is a shortened form of *Eleazar*, which means "God helps." In the first century, it was the fourth most common name for Jewish men (see also {{Luke 16:19-31|Luke 16:19–31}}). 

- Bethany was a small village east of Jerusalem, just past the Mount of Olives ({{John 11:18|John 11:18}}). Jesus often stayed there when he visited Jerusalem. He likely traveled through Bethany on his way to Jerusalem. This was because most Jews from Galilee took a route going south to Jericho, then west to Jerusalem. 

- Mary and Martha were sisters (see {{Luke 10:38-42|Luke 10:38–42}}). Martha was probably older. She was the host in Luke’s Gospel and represented the family. Mary later anointed Jesus with perfume ({{John 12:1-8|John 12:1–8}}).

Jesus was close friends with Mary, Martha and Lazarus. Yet he didn’t hurry to heal Lazarus when Mary and Martha sent for him.

Instead he told his disciples that he would raise Lazarus from the dead. This would be his seventh sign in John’s gospel. It would show people God’s plan for the resurrection.

Jesus told the disciples there wasn’t much daylight left. He meant that there wasn’t much time left for him to do God’s work. Jesus is God’s Light but he wouldn’t be in the world much longer.

It was dangerous for Jesus to go south into Judea where Lazarus was. The Jewish leaders there wanted to kill him. The disciples didn’t understand why Jesus was going there or what he was going to do. But they followed him into danger anyway.

The resurrection of Lazarus points to the future death and resurrection of Jesus. The description of Lazarus’s tomb is similar to the description of the tomb Jesus was placed in after he died ({{John 11:38|11:38}}, {{John 11:44|44}}; {{John 20:1|20:1}}, {{John 20:7|7}}). Both accounts mention a cave and burial cloths. These details connect the two events and help us see that Lazarus’s story is a sign.

Soon after Lazarus was raised, a woman anointed Jesus for burial ({{John 12:3|12:3}}). This act prepared him for his coming death.

Then the time for his glorification began ({{John 12:23|12:23}}).
The two sisters had a difficult choice to make. They knew Jesus was able to heal, but they also realized that his return to Judea would involve personal risk ({{John 11:8|11:8}}).

Jesus responded with words that were similar to his words about the man born blind ({{John 9:1-5|9:1–5}}). Jesus already knew Lazarus was dead ({{John 11:14|11:14}}). He was talking about Lazarus's resurrection, which would bring glory to God ({{John 11:43|11:43}}).

The trip to Bethany from where Jesus was staying would have taken only one day (see {{John 10:40|10:40}}). However, Jesus followed his own timing and did not let others rush him ({{John 2:4|2:4}}; {{John 7:5-9|7:5–9}}).
The disciples were rightly worried about the risk (see {{John 7:25|7:25}}; {{John 8:37|8:37}}, {{John 8:44|44}}, {{John 8:59|59}}; {{John 10:31|10:31}}, {{John 10:39|39}}).

- *Thomas*: See also {{John 14:5|14:5}}; {{John 20:24|20:24}}; {{John 21:2|21:2}}; {{Mark 3:18|Mark 3:18}}. 

- *Let us also go, so that we may die*: Thomas knew that earlier visits to Judea had been risky ({{John 5:18|John 5:18}}; {{John 10:31|10:31}}, {{John 10:39|39}}). Traveling to Jerusalem now would likely mean death for Jesus (compare {{John 11:49-50|11:49–50}}).

In Jewish custom at that time, people were usually buried on the same day they died. Families placed the body in a tomb quickly, often within hours.

John tells us that Lazarus had been in the tomb for four days. This detail is important. It shows that Lazarus was truly dead.

Because four days had passed, this miracle was not a simple resuscitation (bringing someone back who only seemed dead). Jesus did not restore a weak person who might recover. He raised a man who had been dead and buried for several days.

Martha and Jesus talked about people rising from the dead. Martha’s words showed what many Jews at that time thought resurrection meant. The common belief was that God’s people would be rescued by him on the last day. The last day was another name for judgement day. He would raise up the dead who had been faithful to him.

That was the hope that Martha spoke about. Jesus boldly said, I am the resurrection and the life. This was Jesus’ fifth I am statement in John’s gospel. Jesus makes the hope of resurrection come true. Those who follow him faithfully will live for ever after their bodies die. This is because Jesus will raise his people from the dead in the new creation.

Martha believed what Jesus said about himself. She believed he is the Messiah and the Son of God. Martha was the fifth witness to Jesus in John’s gospel. To help others believe him, Jesus called Lazarus out of the tomb. Raising Lazarus from the dead was the seventh sign Jesus did. The crying and sadness over Lazarus’ death stopped. Many people believed in Jesus when they saw this sign.

Life in New Testament times was lived publicly. Lazarus’s large extended family, as well as the villagers, had arrived for a seven-day mourning period. To console the sisters in their loss, there was great wailing and crying (see {{John 11:33|11:33}} and corresponding study note).

*Lord, if You had been here*: Mary later repeated Martha’s words ({{John 11:32|11:32}}), because both sisters knew that Jesus had a reputation as a healer. They concluded that Jesus would have healed Lazarus, but they did not imagine that Jesus would restore him from death.

*whatever You ask of Him*: Martha believed Jesus could still help in some way. Despite this, she objected when Jesus wanted to open the tomb ({{John 11:39|11:39}}). She did not think Jesus would resurrect her brother from the dead.

*rise again in the resurrection at the last day*: Martha misunderstood Jesus because she thought he meant the general resurrection of all dead people at the end of time (compare {{John 11:11-13|11:11–13}}).

- Jesus helped Martha believe in him not only as someone who heals, but as someone who defeats death. 

- *I am the resurrection and the life*: Victory over death comes from living in union with Jesus. Although the followers of Jesus will one day die, they will have eternal life after death. For more on the *I am* statements of Jesus, see the study note on 6:35.

- *Do you believe this?*: Jesus was not simply asking Martha if he could bring Lazarus out of the grave. Martha already believed that Lazarus would rise again on the last day.

Instead, Jesus asked a deeper question. Did Martha believe that life itself is connected to him?

- “*Yes, Lord*”: Even though she did not fully understand, she acknowledged that Jesus was the Christ, God's chosen one. But she was still surprised by his power.
Mary now joined the scene on the edge of the village, repeating her sister’s cry of misery. She fell at the feet of Jesus, not in worship but in desperate grief.

- Loud *weeping* and crying out were common public displays of grief in this culture, as was beating one's chest ({{Mark 5:38|Mark 5:38}}; {{Luke 18:13|Luke 18:13}}). 

- The Greek word translated *deeply moved in spirit* describes strong human emotion, including outrage or anger. Jesus was not angry at Martha or Mary. Jesus was angry because the situation showed the people’s lack of belief, even though resurrection was real and near.

Lazarus was buried in a tomb cut from the rocky hillside; such tombs were common. The tomb was closed and opened for further burials with a rolling stone that covered the entrance. A central door led to a cave room where burial benches were carved in stone along the inner wall. Horizontal burial chambers were cut along the top edge of the benches.

News of the miracle quickly spread to Jerusalem ({{John 12:9|12:9}}, {{John 12:17|17}}). Again, people had different opinions about who Jesus was ({{John 6:66-69|6:66–69}}; {{John 7:43|7:43}}; {{John 9:16|9:16}}; {{John 10:19|10:19}}; {{John 11:37|11:37}}). Jesus was famous in Galilee for healing and raising the dead (see {{Matthew 9:24-26|Matthew 9:24–26}}; {{Matthew 10:8|10:8}}; {{Matthew 11:5|11:5}}). Now he had brought this power to Judea.

The Sanhedrin heard about Lazarus. They thought that to protect the Jewish faith they had to stop Jesus.

The high priest Caiaphas spoke words that were truer than he knew. Jesus would die for the nation but not in the way that Caiaphas thought. Jesus’ death would bring life to the world.

Jesus would bring together into one family all who follow God anywhere in the world. Many people were looking for Jesus. The Jewish leaders wanted to arrest him. The crowds wondered if he would teach and do mighty works at the Passover Feast.

The council met to discuss what to do about Jesus. During their discussion, they revealed their fear. They were afraid that everyone would believe in him.

If many people believed that Jesus was the Messiah (God’s chosen one), this could cause political trouble. In that time, the Romans ruled over Judea. They did not tolerate leaders who claimed to be kings.

The Romans viewed Jewish messiahs with suspicion. They feared rebellion. The council worried that the growing movement around Jesus might lead the Romans to attack Jerusalem and destroy the temple.

So their concern was not only religious. It was also political. They feared losing their place, their authority, and even their nation.
Caiaphas was the ruler of the high council from AD 18–36. He worked for ten years alongside Pontius Pilate, governor of Judea (AD 26–36; see {{John 18:29|18:29}}), keeping the peace with Rome.

*it is better … that one man die*: Caiaphas spoke with clear political intent. He argued that it was better for one man to die than for the whole nation to suffer. He meant that it was better for Jesus, whom he saw as a threat, to die than for Rome to destroy the Jewish people.

Caiaphas viewed Jesus as a possible revolutionary. He feared that Rome would crush the nation if unrest grew. From his point of view, sacrificing one man would protect many.

But his words carried a deeper meaning. Caiaphas did not understand this meaning. In a way he could not see, he spoke the truth. Jesus would die for the people. His death would bring salvation (rescue from sin and separation from God).

John explains that Caiaphas did not speak on his own authority. As high priest that year, he spoke prophetically (as one who speaks a message from God). God used his words to point to the saving purpose of the death of Jesus.

The rescue that God’s people needed was not mainly from Rome. It would come through the cross of Christ.
Christ’s death was not for Israel only, but for all, including people of other cultures all across the world ({{John 10:16|10:16}}; {{John 12:32|12:32}}).

- When the Jewish leaders started planning to kill Jesus, Jesus responded carefully ({{John 11:54|11:54}}). He did not act in fear, but he acted wisely. He chose to leave the area for a time.

- *Ephraim* was a village about 19 kilometers (12 miles) north of Jerusalem. Jesus was safe there from the Sanhedrin but close enough to walk to the Passover feast that was happening soon ({{John 11:55|11:55}}).

As crowds arrived in Jerusalem on pilgrimage for Passover (see {{John 2:13|2:13}}), the city was buzzing with talk about Jesus and his miracle of raising Lazarus from the dead. People wondered if Jesus would be obedient to the law and come to the city to celebrate or play it safe in the countryside. The priests and Pharisees knew that Jesus was faithful to the law and would attend the festival, so they tried to make the city a trap for him.

Pilgrims from throughout Israel began arriving in Jerusalem the week before the Passover. The festival was on Thursday that year. Jesus arrived in the area late on the previous Friday, just before the Sabbath.

At the beginning of the last week of his life, Jesus returned to Bethany.

His friends Mary, Martha and Lazarus invited many people to celebrate Jesus at a meal.

Mary and Judas treated Jesus very differently.

Mary honoured Jesus with an expensive gift that showed her deep love. Judas did the opposite. He wanted the money from the expensive gift for himself.

Jesus explained that Mary wasn’t wasting money. She was helping to prepare him for his death.

Many people believed that Jesus was God’s Son because they saw that Lazarus was alive again.

The religious leaders wanted that to stop happening. So they planned to kill Lazarus.

- In this part of John’s Gospel, two stories move forward at the same time.

First, more and more people begin to praise Jesus. Their excitement reaches a high point when crowds welcome him into Jerusalem with shouts of joy ({{John 12:12-13|12:12–13}}).

Second, the religious authorities become more determined to arrest Jesus and put him to death. As public support grows, their opposition grows as well.

- John's Gospel describes three events that happened only days before Passover ({{John 12:1-11|12:1–11}}, {{John 12:12-19|12–19}}, {{John 12:20-36|20–36}}). Then he explains why most of the people refused to believe and describes the final public message spoken by Jesus ({{John 12:37-50|12:37–50}}).
*those reclining*: People usually sat or leaned back at a low table while eating.

- *Mary … anointed Jesus' feet*. This was not awkward because Jews reclined at formal meals, but it was still a dramatic gesture (compare {{Matthew 26:6-16|Matthew 26:6–16}}; {{Mark 14:3-9|Mark 14:3–9}}). 

- Nard was a valuable spice from North India. It was sweet, red, and smelled like the perfume made from the gladiola plant. Twelve ounces of nard cost one year's wages ({{John 12:5|John 12:5}}). 

According to Mark's Gospel, Mary also anointed the head of Jesus ({{Mark 14:3|Mark 14:3}}). The perfume ran down and made his clothes smell good ({{Mark 14:8|Mark 14:8}}).

- *her hair*: Women never took their hair covering off in public (see {{Luke 7:38|Luke 7:38}}). Mary was acting with deep and costly devotion.
*three hundred denarii*: Judas may have been exaggerating, but Mary’s sacrifice was certainly very costly.

*Leave her alone*: Jesus defended Mary by explaining her actions. The nard was a burial spice for his death. Jesus was readied for burial as he approached the hour of glorification and death (see study note on 12:23).

Jesus would not ignore the poor. He cared deeply for people in need.

However, this moment to honor and serve him was unique. It was a special opportunity that would not happen again.

- The next day was Sunday (see {{John 12:1|12:1}}). 

- A large crowd of religious travelers, many from Galilee, camped in this area. As Jesus traveled the road to Jerusalem, they cheered for him. This triumphal entry appears in all four Gospels ({{Matthew 21:1-11|Matthew 21:1–11}}; {{Mark 11:1-11|Mark 11:1–11}}; {{Luke 19:29-38|Luke 19:29–38}}).

Jesus entered Jerusalem like a king taking part in a victory parade. The disciples didn’t understand all of the prophecies about Jesus in the Old Testament. Much later they understood how Jesus’ actions fulfilled those prophecies.

The crowd greeted Jesus with shouts and called him their king. The Jewish leaders were angry that more and more people were following Jesus. Even people who weren’t Jews wanted to see Jesus. Jesus wanted everyone to follow him. This included Greeks (Greece).

Jesus knew that soon he would die. He was troubled about the suffering he was about to face. He described his death as being lifted up from the earth. He was talking about dying on the cross. When that happened, the power of evil would be broken. The prince of this world is another name for the devil. The prince would no longer rule the world because Jesus would start ruling as King.

God spoke out loud to answer Jesus’ prayer. The crowd was confused about the voice from heaven. They were also confused about why Jesus was talking about death. Jesus didn’t explain things to them plainly. He only reminded them that he was the Light that the world needed.

- *Palm branches*: The date *palm* symbolized pride in the Jewish nation and celebration. 

- *meet Him*: The Greek word often describes crowds welcoming a king returning in triumph from a war. 

- *Blessed is He*: The crowd quoted {{Psalm 118:25-26|Psalm 118:25–26}}, with a greeting for those who came to Jerusalem. 

The phrase "*Blessed is the King of Israel!*" is not in the psalm (but see {{Zephaniah 3:15|Zephaniah 3:15}}). Although the people saw Jesus as a national political liberator, he rejected this role ({{John 6:15|John 6:15}}).

By choosing *a young donkey* instead of a warhorse, Jesus calmed the excited crowd that was eager for him to become king. He also fulfilled Old Testament prophecies about the Messiah (see {{Zechariah 9:9|Zechariah 9:9}}). He made it clear that his kingship was not based on violence. He did not come as a warrior to conquer nations. He came to give life. His rule would bring peace, not military victory.

The crowds did not fully understand who Jesus was. Even his disciples did not grasp the full meaning of what was happening. They saw the events, but they did not yet understand their true significance (their deeper meaning).

After Jesus was glorified (raised up in death, resurrection, and return to the Father), things changed. When the disciples received the Holy Spirit, they began to understand more clearly (see {{John 2:22|2:22}}).
This scene describes the highest point of the popularity of Jesus. At this time, large crowds followed him. Many people were excited about his teaching and his miracles.

*the whole world *(literally *the world*): The Pharisees' words were more meaningful than they realized. Jesus came to reach the world ({{John 3:17|3:17}}), and the Pharisees said that Jesus had accomplished his task.

Among those people attracted to Jesus were some Greeks who believed in Israel's God. They had come to the Passover feast to worship ({{John 12:19|12:19}}). The mission of Jesus was not only for Israel but for the entire world ({{John 10:16|10:16}}; {{John 11:52|11:52}}). After the resurrection of Jesus, the church's mission was to go beyond Judea to Samaria, and even to the ends of the earth ({{Matthew 28:19|Matthew 28:19}}; {{Acts 1:8|Acts 1:8}}).
The Greeks approached Philip because he had a Greek name and was most likely also Greek.

Jesus often said that *the hour *had not yet come ({{John 2:4|2:4}}; {{John 7:30|7:30}}; {{John 8:20|8:20}}), but now it had. The arrival of the Greeks marked the beginning of the most important moment in the ministry of Jesus. This was the time of his glorification.

This happened when the saving work of Jesus on the cross was completed. He rose from the dead, gave the Holy Spirit, and returned to his place of glory in heaven ({{John 19:30|19:30}}; {{John 20:1-31|20:1–31}}; {{John 20:22|20:22}}; {{John 17:5|17:5}}, {{John 17:11|11}}). 

The connection with the Greeks who had come to Jerusalem was important ({{John 12:20|12:20}}). The public ministry of Jesus among the Jews was coming to an end. His mission was not limited to one nation. Through his death and resurrection, he would belong to the whole world.
The central event of the glorification of Jesus was the cross ({{John 12:23|12:23}}). Like a *kernel of wheat* planted in the soil, the death of Jesus would bring abundant life.

For disciples (followers of Jesus), sacrifice and self-effacement (choosing not to put oneself first) are part of this path. They do not lose life by following Jesus. Instead, they gain the fullness of life that comes through his sacrifice.

Those who renounce (turn away from) the world’s priorities will be with Jesus forever. God will honor those who serve his Son. In this way, the path of humble obedience leads to eternal life and honor.

*My soul is troubled*: John used the same term (Greek *tarassō*) to describe the strong emotion of agony that Jesus felt when he stood before Lazarus’s tomb ({{John 11:33|11:33}}; also {{John 13:21|13:21}}). 

When Jesus faced his coming death, he was not without emotion. He did not act as if nothing troubled him. He experienced real anguish (deep sorrow and distress). Even in his distress, Jesus remained obedient to the Father’s will. Throughout his ministry, he had said that he did only what the Father sent him to do ({{John 5:19-23|5:19–23}}; {{John 6:37|6:37}}; {{John 8:29|8:29}}, {{John 8:38|38}}; {{John 14:31|14:31}}).

- *A voice came from heaven*: Compare {{Matthew 3:17|Matthew 3:17}}; {{Matthew 17:5|17:5}}; {{Mark 1:11|Mark 1:11}}; {{Mark 9:7|9:7}}; {{Luke 3:22|Luke 3:22}}; {{Luke 9:35|9:35}}. 

- God had already brought glory to himself when Christ entered the world, and through the work of Jesus. This showed God's power to the world ({{John 1:14|John 1:14}}). 

- *I will glorify it again*: The final display of glory would come at the cross (see {{John 12:23|12:23}}; {{John 17:1|17:1}}). In John's Gospel, the cross is an event of glory as Christ was "lifted up" and glorified there ({{John 12:32|12:32}}). 

Jesus was prepared for crucifixion like a king coming to his coronation. The cross was like a throne (see {{John 19:19-22|19:19–22}}). They buried Jesus like a king. 

- The time of his glorification included all the events from his arrest through his resurrection.

It was impossible for people to comprehend what was happening with Jesus, and many of his signs led to confusion and division in the crowd. Only later did his disciples understand ({{John 2:22|2:22}}; {{John 12:16|12:16}}), when Jesus was glorified and the Spirit was given. Still, God’s voice symbolized his validation of his Son before the world.

- In John’s Gospel, judgment does not happen only on the final Judgment Day. It began when Jesus came into the world as the light ({{John 3:19|3:19}}; {{John 5:24|5:24}}; {{John 9:39|9:39}}). 

- Satan is *the prince of this world.* Satan promotes darkness, leads people into sin, and spreads death. Although Satan’s final defeat is still future, his power was broken through the work of Jesus (see {{Luke 10:17-18|Luke 10:17–18}}; {{Mark 3:27|Mark 3:27}}). 

Now Christ reigns as king in heaven ({{Acts 7:55-56|Acts 7:55–56}}; {{Ephesians 1:19-22|Ephesians 1:19–22}}).

*when I am lifted up from the earth* (see {{John 3:14|3:14}}; {{John 8:28|8:28}}): The crowd did not understand what Jesus meant. The Greek verb can also mean "be exalted" ({{Matthew 23:12|Matthew 23:12}}). Or, it can refer to honor ({{Luke 10:15|Luke 10:15}}). In John's Gospel, the cross was not a place of shame for Jesus, but where his true glory was shown.

- Many people in the time of Jesus believed that the Messiah would live forever and defeat his enemies. They expected a strong and victorious ruler.

Because of this belief, the words Jesus spoke confused them.

- *Who is this Son of Man?*: The Jews did not understand what sort of Messiah planned to die.

- Jesus was *the Light* ({{John 1:4|1:4}}, {{John 1:7-9|7–9}}; {{John 3:19-21|3:19–21}}; {{John 8:12|8:12}}). He urged the crowd to choose to believe in him before it was too late. 

- They could *become sons of the light* by being spiritually born through God's power ({{John 1:12-13|1:12–13}}). 

- *was hidden from them*: He first withdrew from Judea and then from this audience ({{John 11:54|11:54}}; {{John 12:36|12:36}}). Soon, he would withdraw from the world ({{John 17:11|17:11}}).
Jesus finished his work, but they still did not believe in him. His sermons before the world were complete and the signs had been displayed, but he was rejected ({{John 1:11|1:11}}).

John ended the first half of his gospel by writing about seeing and believing. He also wrote about light and darkness. Jesus is the Light of the world. Some people believe Jesus is who he said he was. They are in his Light and can see.

People who don’t believe in Jesus are in darkness. They are blind. Many people had seen the signs Jesus did. But they didn't believe he was God's Son. It was like they were blind and couldn’t see who he really was.

Certain Jewish leaders believed in him but didn’t follow him in public. To receive what God wants to give them, people must believe that Jesus is God’s Son. They must hear what he says and then they must trust and obey him. They must be committed to following him.

This is the what the good news about Jesus requires people to do. Those who refuse to obey Jesus will be judged one day. When someone obeys Jesus they are obeying God. That is how people receive eternal life that will never be destroyed.

*they were unable to believe*: John quotes {{Isaiah 6:10|Isaiah 6:10}} to explain Israel's lack of belief (see {{Matthew 13:13-15|Matthew 13:13–15}}; {{Mark 4:12|Mark 4:12}}; {{Luke 8:10|Luke 8:10}}; {{Acts 28:26-27|Acts 28:26–27}}). When God's revelation comes, we must believe. If we refuse, the light disappears ({{John 12:35-36|John 12:35–36}}). When God’s light departs, the darkness closes over unbelieving hearts. This means that continued rejection leads to deeper spiritual blindness.
The prophet Isaiah had seen the glory of the Messiah and how the world would respond (see {{Isaiah 6:10|Isaiah 6:10}}).

Many people did believe in Jesus. However, they were afraid to admit it in public.

They feared the reaction of the religious leaders and the social consequences that might follow.

To follow Jesus means more than private belief. It includes openly identifying with him and telling others about him, even when this may bring rejection ({{John 1:35-51|1:35–51}}; {{John 4:1-42|4:1–42}}).

Jesus makes a final appeal for faith in him. These verses summarize chapters {{John 1:1-12:50|1–12}}. The Father sent Jesus, who is the only source of his ministry. Jesus is the light shining in darkness to bring salvation and eternal life to all who believe in him.
The greatest error is for people to see the light and reject it, thinking it has no connection with the Father who sent the light.

Jesus’ last meal with the disciples was right before the Passover Feast. During the meal Jesus did something to show how deeply he loved them. He became like a humble slave and washed his disciples’ feet.

Jesus did this even for the disciple who would hand him over to his enemies. Jesus washed his disciples’ feet to give them an example. He wanted them to understand what it means to serve others with love.

Jesus is the Leader who serves. He is the King who is also God’s servant. Those who follow him must practice this same love and service.

The setting is the final Passover meal of Jesus on Thursday evening. During this meal, Judas Iscariot betrays Jesus. John does not describe the meal itself like the Synoptic Gospels do ({{Matthew 26:17-29|Matthew 26:17–29}}; {{Mark 14:12-25|Mark 14:12–25}}; {{Luke 22:7-20|Luke 22:7–20}}; see also {{1 Corinthians 11:23-26|1 Corinthians 11:23–26}}). John focuses on other activities at the event, such as:

- the foot washing ({{John 13:1-17|John 13:1–17}}), 

- Judas’s betrayal ({{John 13:18-30|13:18–30}}), and 

- the prediction of Peter’s denials ({{John 13:31-38|13:31–38}}).

This section focuses on the sign of the cross, the great climax of the life of Jesus, as well as the time Jesus spent preparing his disciples for it (chapters {{John 13:1-17:26|13–17}}). Each event during these important days glorified Jesus. His arrest, trial, death on the cross, and resurrection all bring forth responses of awe. On the cross, Jesus is "lifted up" in glory before the world ({{John 12:32|12:32}}).
*Judas … Iscariot*: He had refused to trust in Jesus. Darkness consumed him and he became a tool of the devil (compare study note on 12:39–40).

Foot washing was common in Greek and Jewish cultures as a daily routine. It was also a common gesture when hosting guests (see {{Luke 7:36-50|Luke 7:36–50}}). It was a humble task designated for servants. When Jesus began to wash the disciples’ feet, he assumed the role of a servant.

Knowing how committed Peter was to Jesus, it makes sense that he protested. However, Jesus was not just showing Peter how to serve. This was a symbolic introduction of the greater sacrifice Jesus would make on the cross ({{John 13:7|13:7}}). Receiving spiritual cleansing from Jesus is necessary for discipleship. If Peter could not accept this act, he could not be a disciple of Jesus.

*my hands and my head as well*: Peter misunderstood Jesus (compare {{John 2:19-20|2:19–20}}; {{John 3:3-4|3:3–4}}). Peter thought having more water meant having more of Jesus. Everything became obvious to Peter only when he received the Holy Spirit (for example, see {{Acts 2:14-36|Acts 2:14–36}}).

Jesus was pointing to a deeper cleansing through his sacrifice.

He was not speaking only about washing the body. He was speaking about being made clean in a complete way.

Through his death, he makes a person clean all over. This means forgiveness of sin and a restored relationship with God.

- Jesus performed acts of humble service, such as washing his disciples’ feet and giving his life on the cross. By doing this, he set an example for others to follow. He showed that true greatness is expressed through love, service, and personal sacrifice for others.

- *wash one another's feet*: Foot washing was a common act in that culture. Because of this, some think that Jesus meant for his followers to repeat this action in a literal way. Others believe he used it as a symbol of humble service.

In either case, the main point is clear. Jesus wants his followers to serve others with humility and self-giving love. Servanthood and sacrifice should mark their lives.

*no servant is greater than his master*: This saying was popular and appears in a number of passages (see also {{John 15:20|15:20}}; {{Matthew 10:24|Matthew 10:24}}; {{Luke 6:40|Luke 6:40}}). Here, Jesus meant that the servant should follow the master's example of sacrifice.

- *I am not speaking about all of you*: This is the third time Jesus mentions that Judas will betray him ({{John 13:2|13:2}}, {{John 13:11|11}}). This matter deeply "troubled" Jesus ({{John 13:21|13:21}}). 

- *I know whom I have chosen*: This does not mean Jesus only chose the 11 disciples and excluded Judas. Jesus chose Judas and gave him every opportunity to believe. He realized that Judas had chosen the darkness instead of the light ({{John 6:70|6:70}}).

- *The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me*: Eating together was a cultural symbol of personal intimacy, which made Judas’s betrayal all the more serious.

Jesus was troubled in his spirit. One of his closest followers was going to hand him over to his enemies. Another follower would say that he didn’t know Jesus.

Jesus tried to explain to his disciples what would happen and what he was feeling. But they didn’t understand. They couldn’t imagine that Judas would turn against Jesus. Peter couldn’t imagine that he wouldn’t always follow Jesus.

Jesus warned them before all these things happened. Later his warning would help them to believe that he always spoke the truth. He also gave the disciples instructions about how to treat each other. Even though they would face problems, they were to love one another.

Jesus knew that he was obeying his Father. He was about to bring glory to God and accomplish God’s plan. Even in his sadness, Jesus was sure about what he had to do.

- Judas’s betrayal did not surprise Jesus. It should also not surprise his disciples when it happens. 

- *that I am He:* By using the phrase *I am*, Jesus clearly identified himself with the God of the Old Testament. See {{Exodus 3:14|Exodus 3:14}}.
For the third time in the Gospel of John, Jesus *became troubled* (Greek *tarassō*; see {{John 11:33|11:33}}; {{John 12:27|12:27}}). When Judas betrayed Jesus, it caused him deep grief.

- The disciple whom Jesus loved is appears:

- at the cross ({{John 19:26-27|19:26–27}}),

- at the tomb ({{John 20:2-9|20:2–9}}), and

- and at the resurrection ({{John 21:1|21:1}}, {{John 21:20-23|20–23}}). 

He also wrote the Gospel of John ({{John 21:24-25|21:24–25}}). Some scholars believe that Lazarus was in fact the disciple whom Jesus loved (see {{John 11:3|11:3}}, {{John 11:5|5}}, {{John 11:36|36}}). The person referred to here was among the 12 apostles, so most people identify the disciple whom Jesus loved as the apostle John. 

- *was reclining at His side*: They were likely reclining at a *triclinium,* a U-shaped table with couches around it. Guests reclined on the couches, while the center allowed those serving to access them. Those who were eating supported themselves with their left elbows and used their right hands to eat. They extended their feet away from the table (compare {{Luke 7:38|Luke 7:38}}).

Peter told the disciple sitting next to Jesus ("the one whom Jesus loved") to ask who would betray him ({{John 13:23|13:23}}). As the disciple was reclining next to Jesus, he leaned over and spoke to Jesus in private.

Meals included flat bread, which those eating would dip into a shared bowl. Jesus gave a piece to Judas (compare {{Ruth 2:14|Ruth 2:14}}). The disciples might have thought Jesus was honoring him. 

They did not understand what was happening. They even thought that when Judas left, it was to fulfill an official duty for the feast ({{John 13:29|John 13:29}}). However, Jesus was signaling to Judas that he knew Judas's plan and was not surprised. The knowledge Jesus has is deep and complete (see {{John 1:48|1:48}}; {{John 2:25|2:25}}).

- *Satan entered into him*: Judas became an example of what happens to people consumed by the darkness (see {{Luke 22:3|Luke 22:3}}). Satan uses such people as tools in a wider struggle against the light.

- *What you are about to do, do quickly*: By giving this command, Jesus again showed he was in control, not human beings or Satan (see study note on John 7:30).

None of the others suspected that something odd was happening. Passover evening was one of the only nights when the city gates were left open. The night was spent in prayer and meditation, money was given to the poor, and provisions were always needed for this complex meal.

*out into the night*: This detail is more than a note about the time of day. It has symbolic meaning.

Judas’s departure shows his spiritual condition. Darkness had taken hold of him completely (see study note on 13:2; compare {{John 3:19|3:19}}). Jesus, the light of the world, is the opposite of the night.

The time had come. Judas’s departure into the night marked a clear turning point in the story of the Gospel. Jesus was now left with his closest friends, as the hour of his glory was beginning. This period began with Judas’s betrayal and ended with the resurrection.

The Old Testament and later Jewish literature include numerous examples of farewells in which a dying person offers last words to intimate friends (see {{Genesis 49:1-27|Gen 49:1–27}}; {{Deuteronomy 31:1-34:12|Deut 31–34}}; {{Joshua 23:1-24:33|Josh 23–24}}; {{1 Samuel 12:1-25|1 Sam 12}}; {{1 Chronicles 28:1-29:30|1 Chr 28:1–29:30}}). Such farewells used a standard form. The dying person, surrounded by his loved ones, comforted them and exhorted them to obey the law. He prayed and blessed them and often left behind some writings. In some cases, the departing person passed on his “spirit” to his followers or his successor (see {{Numbers 27:18|Num 27:18}}; {{Deuteronomy 34:9|Deut 34:9}}; {{2 Kings 2:9-14|2 Kgs 2:9–14}}). Each of these elements is present in Jesus’ farewell. • This section is often called the Upper Room Discourse, since the meal was taken in an “upstairs room” ({{Luke 22:12|Luke 22:12}}).
Jesus addressed the apostles as his children, marking the start of his farewell address.

The command for the disciples to *love one another* was not new (see {{Leviticus 19:18|Leviticus 19:18}}). However, loving each other as Jesus loved was a dramatic change. Jesus showed his love for God through perfect obedience ({{John 14:31|John 14:31}}). Now, he commanded that disciples show their love for him through committed obedience.

Peter claimed to be ready to die for Jesus. But Peter is well known for denying Jesus ({{John 18:15-18|18:15–18}}, {{John 18:25-27|25–27}}; see also {{Matthew 26:32-34|Matthew 26:32–34}}; {{Mark 14:27-30|Mark 14:27–30}}; {{Luke 22:31-34|Luke 22:31–34}}). Although Peter's courage and loyalty failed, Jesus forgave and restored him ({{John 21:15-19|John 21:15–19}}).

- Jesus felt *troubled* (Greek *tarassō*) on three occasions ({{John 11:33|11:33}}; {{John 12:27|12:27}}; {{John 13:21|13:21}}). His trust in God's power helped him confront these difficult times. When the disciples heard the upsetting words of {{John 13:33|13:33}}, they felt the same way. 

- *believe *(or *trust, *or *have faith*) *in God*: Only trusting God would help them through his hour of death.

Jesus comforted his disciples as he explained that he would be leaving them. But he also promised that they would be together again.

Jesus said I am the way and the truth and the life. This was the sixth time he had described himself using the words I am. Jesus shows the truth about God. He is the way that people can become close to God and have life for ever with God.

Jesus and the Father are joined together through the deepest love. Jesus explained this love by saying that he is in the Father. He explained that the Father is in him as well. They share their deep love with all who obey Jesus.

Jesus promised that the Father would send the Holy Spirit. The Spirit would be a friend who comforted and helped Jesus’ followers. Through the Spirit’s power, Jesus’ followers would continue his work. They would do even more mighty works than when they were together with Jesus. They would pray to him asking him to do his powerful works through them. And they could be sure that he listened and would answer.
Jesus provided answers to his disciples’ many spoken and unspoken concerns.

*In My Father’s house are many rooms*: God's house is where he lives ({{Revelation 21:9-22:5|Revelation 21:9–22:5}}). The Greek word for *rooms* comes from a verb meaning "remain, abide, dwell." Jesus promises his followers a place to live with him, wherever he is. Later, this *house *becomes a spiritual presence. Jesus makes his home in the hearts of his followers through the Holy Spirit ({{John 14:23|John 14:23}}). This means that believers carry God’s presence inside them.

Some scholars think that Jesus meant he would come and get his followers after the resurrection ({{John 14:18|14:18}}). Others think these words refer to the second coming of Jesus. For the disciples, the return of Jesus from the grave was more important (chapter {{John 16:1-33|16}}).

- *I am*: See study note on 6:35. You can only access the Father through Jesus, who is *the way and the truth and the life*. 

- The way to the Father is only through Jesus. Other religions and philosophies suggest different ways to God. But Jesus claimed he is the only way to God. 

- Jesus is *the truth* because God is *truth*. 

- God is the source of eternal life. At Lazarus’s tomb, Jesus demonstrated his divine power over life and death ({{John 11:25|11:25}}).
Philip did not yet understand that in Jesus he was seeing the full embodiment of God ({{John 14:9|14:9}}).

*Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father*: Compare {{John 1:1-2|1:1–2}}. Jesus Christ is God in human body ({{John 1:14|1:14}}). This explains his ability to perform divine works. Jesus did not just teach about God, he is God. Jesus's remarkable statement here echoed what he said at the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah): “I and the Father are one” ({{John 10:30|10:30}}). This claim is the reason for the world's opposition to Christ ({{John 5:18|5:18}}).

Jesus made surprising and powerful claims about himself ({{John 10:30|10:30}}, {{John 10:37-38|37–38}}). However, true faith recognizes the close union between Jesus and God the Father. To believe in Jesus is to trust that he truly reveals and represents the Father.

- Jesus promised that those who believe in him would do great works and pray with confidence (see {{1 John 5:14|1 John 5:14}}). This would happen after Jesus returned to the Father, when he sent the Holy Spirit to give them strength and guidance ({{John 14:16|John 14:16}}). 

- *The greater things* will not surpass what Jesus did. Instead, ordinary people will do these works because the Holy Spirit gives them power. God promised that in the era of the Spirit, he would bring his kingdom and power into the world in a new way.

*If you love me*: Because Jesus loves the Father, he is obedient to what God directs him to say and do ({{John 12:49|12:49}}). If we love him, we will obey him, too ({{John 14:21|14:21}}, {{John 14:23|23}}; {{John 15:10|15:10}}, {{John 15:14|14}}; see {{1 John 2:3-4|1 John 2:3–4}}; {{1 John 5:2|5:2}}).
*another Advocate*: The Spirit continues the work of Jesus by advising, defending, and protecting believers.

*the Spirit of truth*: The Holy *Spirit *communicates the truth about God (see also {{John 15:26|15:26}}; {{John 16:13|16:13}}). The Spirit maintains the presence of Jesus in the world, continuing and supporting the work Jesus began.

Jesus had already assured his followers that they would not be spiritual orphans and that he would return to them ({{John 14:1-4|14:1–4}}). While he is away, they will be filled with the Spirit, who will sustain them with his presence ({{John 14:12-17|14:12–17}}).

The resurrection of Jesus began a new spiritual union with his disciples ({{John 14:19|14:19}}). This union is like the close relationship he has with the Father (see {{John 15:4-5|15:4–5}}; {{1 John 1:3|1 John 1:3}}).

- Several men named Judas appear in the New Testament. Judas, the brother of Jesus, wrote the letter of Jude ({{Mark 6:3|Mark 6:3}}). {{Luke 6:16|Luke 6:16}}lists Judas, the son of James, as a disciple (John mentions this Judas in this verse). He is also known as Thaddaeus ({{Matthew 10:3|Matthew 10:3}}; {{Mark 3:18|Mark 3:18}}). 

- *Lord, why*: Judas asked an important question. If Jesus planned to return powerfully from death, why not use the chance to show himself plainly to the world? Why not prove his power and identity?

Jesus didn’t answer Judas’ question plainly. Instead, he reminded the disciples that he and the Father are one.

Those who love and obey him will share a home with the Father and Jesus. God’s Holy Spirit will teach and guide them.

Jesus gave the disciples the gift of his peace. His peace helps his followers to be strong and brave as they trust him.

The prince of the world is the devil. It was going to seem like the devil had won the victory over Jesus. But Jesus made sure his disciples knew the truth about what was going to happen. The devil couldn’t kill Jesus. Jesus chose to sacrifice his life because he loved and completely obeyed his Father.

Jesus loved the people in the world that the Father had created. So he would save them from evil.

- Jesus answered Judas's question. He said his coming would be a deep spiritual revelation that the world would not understand. 

- The coming of Jesus would happen in three events: 

- his resurrection, 

- the arrival of the Holy Spirit, and 

- his second coming. 

When he comes through the Spirit, he and the Father will live within Christians, making a home with each of them (see study note on 14:2).

- Jesus promised to send the Holy Spirit (see also {{John 14:16|14:16}}; {{John 15:26|15:26}}; {{John 16:7|16:7}}, {{John 16:12-14|12–14}}). 

- *The Holy Spirit … will teach you all things*: The Holy Spirit will teach the disciples everything. He will help them remember the words of Jesus and understand what those words mean. John experienced this help from the Spirit as he wrote his gospel ({{John 2:22|2:22}}). Christians also experience this work of the Spirit as they hear and study the Scriptures.

The Jewish greeting *peace* (Hebrew *shalom*) shows the goal of the work of Jesus on earth: to restore humanity's relationship with God ({{Isaiah 9:6-7|Isaiah 9:6–7}}; {{Isaiah 52:7|52:7}}; {{Isaiah 57:19|57:19}}; {{Romans 5:1|Romans 5:1}}). The resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit helped complete this work ({{John 14:28|John 14:28}}).
*The Father is greater than I am*: See also {{John 5:19-20|5:19–20}}. Jesus is submissive to the Father but is also one with the Father ({{John 10:30|10:30}}).

*the prince of this world*: Satan did not control the events in Jerusalem that led to the cross. The death of Jesus on the cross was not an accident, and Jesus was not a helpless victim. Instead, Jesus obeyed God's plan.

*I am*: See study note on 6:35. The *vine* and *the vineyard* have traditionally represented God’s people. He "plants and tends" them in Israel ({{Psalm 80:8-18|Psalm 80:8–18}}; {{Isaiah 5:1-7|Isaiah 5:1–7}}; {{Jeremiah 2:21|Jeremiah 2:21}}; {{Jeremiah 12:10-11|12:10–11}}; {{Ezekiel 15:1-5|Ezekiel 15:1–5}}; {{Hosea 10:1-2|Hosea 10:1–2}}). When Jesus used this image, he made an important change. He declared that he is the true vine and that a relationship with God requires attachment to him.

Jesus spoke to his disciples about vines and branches. He said I am the true vine. This was his last I am statement in John’s gospel.

Jesus wants his followers to remain connected to him like branches are to a vine. That is the only way they can bear the fruit that God wants from them. That fruit is love for each other. It’s also doing the works that Jesus did as he taught and served people.

Jesus was teaching the disciples his way of love. His way is to give his own life for others. He trusted the disciples as his friends. He shared with them the love between the Father and himself.

But Jesus warned them about people who don’t love God. Those who don’t love Jesus don’t love God. They won’t love Jesus’ followers either. Jesus didn’t want the disciples to be surprised when some people hated them. When that happened, the Holy Spirit would help them. The Spirit would be their friend like Jesus was their friend.

Jesus prepared his disciples for his departure, instructing them to remain in close fellowship with him. The image of a grapevine illustrates both intimacy and fruitfulness. To sustain genuine spiritual life in the world, believers must remain intimately connected to Christ.
Gardeners cut away dead branches and trim healthy branches so they will produce more fruit. Fruitfulness is the result of life-giving connection to the vine.

The term *remain* (Greek *menō*) is important for understanding {{John 15:4-10|15:4–10}}. A growing disciple, in whom the Father and the Son live through the Spirit, must be continuously connected to Christ (see {{John 14:16-25|14:16–25}}; {{John 15:26|15:26}}).

*\*Anyone who does not remain in Christ is separated from the vine and its life. A living branch produces clusters of grapes ({{John 15:5|15:5}}). Connection with the vine allows the life of Jesus to flow fruitfully through the disciple. Those who claim to be attached to Christ but yield no fruit are useless and will be burned.
Those whose lives are in harmony with Jesus may ask for anything because their prayers are controlled by his word. Their prayers will be answered and bring glory to God ({{John 14:10-13|14:10–13}}).
True disciples will experience a transformed, fruit-bearing life because they live in a relationship of love with both Jesus and the Father ({{John 15:9-10|15:9–10}}).

Just as Jesus demonstrated his love for the Father by obeying his will ({{John 14:31|14:31}}), the disciples of Jesus show their love by obeying him ({{John 13:34-35|13:34–35}}; {{John 14:15|14:15}}; {{1 John 2:5|1 John 2:5}}; {{1 John 5:2-3|5:2–3}}).

- *This is My commandment … love each other:* See {{John 13:34|13:34}}. 

- Jesus demonstrated his love by sacrificing his life at the cross.

God considered Abraham and Moses to be his friends ({{Exodus 33:11|Exodus 33:11}}; {{2 Chronicles 20:7|2 Chronicles 20:7}}; {{Isaiah 41:8|Isaiah 41:8}}; {{James 2:23|James 2:23}}). This is the closest relationship possible between God and a person. Jesus chooses his friends ({{John 15:16|John 15:16}}). They demonstrate their friendship by obeying him.
The disciples of a rabbi were considered his servants or slaves. Jesus elevated his followers to a higher relationship as his friends.

Disciples must be like their master in every way. They must show love and obedience and experience opposition from those against their message ({{John 15:20-21|15:20–21}}; see {{John 9:1-41|9:1–41}}; {{John 11:16|11:16}}). Darkness opposes light ({{John 1:5|1:5}}). The followers of Jesus carry that light in the world ({{1 John 1:7|1 John 1:7}}; {{1 John 2:9|2:9}}). They should expect the world to hate them in the way it hated Jesus (see {{John 17:14|John 17:14}}). The disciples of Jesus share his separation from and conflict with the world.
*No servant is greater than his master*: See study note on 13:16. The disciples of Jesus should live like him in every way, even when they face suffering or death because of their faith.

*Now, however, they have no excuse*: The ministry of Jesus provided both words and works as evidence that pointed to God ({{John 15:22|15:22}}; {{John 15:24|15:24}}). Once people have heard and seen him, they are accountable.
*They hated Me without reason*: This Old Testament citation shows the unjustified anger of people who live in the darkness, meaning those who oppose God’s truth.
*When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth*: Like a legal representative, the Holy Spirit is counselor and protector of the followers of Jesus.
Disciples are not alone when they testify about Christ ({{Matthew 28:20|Matthew 28:20}}). The Holy Spirit is with them and gives them the words to say ({{Matthew 10:19-20|Matthew 10:19–20}}).

Jesus had described the coming conflicts so the disciples would not abandon their faith (literally *be caused to stumble *({{John 15:18-25|15:18–25}}). The biggest challenge they would encounter was rejecting their faith in front of their opponents (see {{Matthew 23:34|Matthew 23:34}}; {{Luke 6:22|Luke 6:22}}). This would especially be true during the difficult times ahead (see {{John 12:35|John 12:35}}; {{1 John 2:9-11|1 John 2:9–11}}).

Jesus warned the disciples that they would be treated badly after he was gone.

This made the disciples very sad.

But Jesus promised that when he left the Holy Spirit would come. He would be a wonderful gift for Jesus’ followers.

The Spirit would show that Jesus was telling the truth about the Father. The Holy Spirit would also show people their sin.

He would help them see that they weren’t living how Jesus taught them to live. He would also show them that the devil didn’t have power over them anymore.

He would be with Jesus’ followers as a true friend. Through the Holy Spirit Jesus’ followers would stay joined to Jesus and the Father.

*the Advocate*: This title refers to the Holy Spirit. The word can mean helper, comforter, or one who speaks on behalf of another.

Jesus taught that the Spirit would come after his departure and glorification (his death, resurrection, and return to the Father; see {{John 7:37-39|7:37–39}}; {{John 14:16|14:16}}, {{John 14:26|26}}; {{John 15:26|15:26}}; {{John 16:12-14|16:12–14}}).

The Spirit was a promised gift. After Jesus returned to the Father, the Spirit would guide, teach, and strengthen his followers.

The Holy Spirit unveils to the world:

- the real nature of its sin, 

- the truth about righteousness found only in God, and 

- the coming judgment.

In one sense, this judgment has already begun. When God’s light shines into the darkness, it exposes what is wrong and calls people to respond.

One of the Spirit’s roles is to convict the world. Convict is a legal term: The world had conducted its trial of Jesus, examining the evidence for his case (his signs and claims). Now the world would stand trial before the Spirit, and its guilt would be proven.

The judgment of sinners had already started. This was because God had already judged the prince of this world, Satan (see {{John 12:31|12:31}}). The world believed it was judging Jesus, but the opposite was true.

- The Spirit of truth, who brings truth from God, guides the judgment of the world. 

- The Spirit speaks only what he hears from the Father. The Father, Son, and Spirit work in perfect unity ({{John 16:15|16:15}}). The disciples could expect the Spirit to reveal new things about the present and future (see {{John 14:26|14:26}}).

Jesus reassured the disciples that his departure (on the cross) would be short and his return (in the resurrection) would be soon. When they saw him again, the disciples would experience overwhelming joy and intimacy with him in the Spirit.

Jesus told the disciples that they would be sad when he was gone. And then they would see him again and be happy.

The disciples didn’t understand what Jesus meant about dying and then coming back to life. But later they would remember his words and be full of joy.

Then they would believe Jesus fully. And they would fully trust God’s love for them.

They would remember what Jesus taught them and boldly pray to God as their Father. They would ask him for everything they needed and know that he would answer.

Jesus’ main message was that the disciples didn’t have to be afraid. They could have peace even when their lives were filled with trouble and hardship.

This is because Jesus is stronger than everything that opposes God. He described this as having won the battle over the world.
